blocks.h: A HOUSE BELOW SEA LEVEL, RENT PAID IN SALT
Roya Publication No. 105
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

Juno Marrow repossesses cars in Bakersfield and sleeps in whichever one she towed that week. She is twenty-seven, quick with her fists and quicker with her mouth, and she has a voicemail on her phone that she has not played in two years.

Abe Coldiron is fifty-one. He fixes air conditioners in Barstow and runs across deserts for no money and no audience. His heart stopped once, nineteen years ago, in the middle of nowhere. He has never asked anyone for help, and he says it is the only record he still holds.
They meet at a gas station in Baker, under the tallest thermometer in the world, when Juno breaks into his truck and finds him sitting in it.

Abe is about to walk the route of 1849 — the true story of two young men who walked out of Death Valley to find help for the families trapped there. His rule is simple. Two go out. Two come back. His partner has quit. He offers Juno a deal: walk with him, and nobody she is hiding from will ever find her out there.
She says she is hiding from nobody. He says then she will love it.

On the first night out, lying on the salt, they find that they have both been dead once, briefly, and that each of them saw the same room. Below sea level, in the lowest place in the country, the room is waiting for them again.
And the walk out was never the hard part.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

This book began with a man I have never met, saying something on a screen that I could not stop thinking about. David Goggins says the mind quits long before the body has to. He says the only way to grow is to go to the place you most want to leave, and stay there until it stops being a visit. The science agrees with the first part.

I wanted to write about that place. Not a lesson on how to get through it. I wanted to write about what the place is like from inside. What the mind says to the body to get it out. How reasonable it sounds. How it shows you water that is not there. And what happens to a person who is made to stay long enough that the voice runs out of things to say.

I gave the place a name, and I took the name from a sign. At Badwater, in Death Valley, a small sign is bolted high on the rock above the salt. It says SEA LEVEL. You stand far beneath it and look up. Nothing that flows into that valley ever flows out. It leaves only by burning off, and what it leaves behind is salt.

There are two kinds of scar in this book, the kind you get in the body and the kind you carry in your head. I wanted a man who is at home in the first and a woman who is at home in the second, and I wanted each of them to find the other’s door. The research on how men and women meet pain is real, and it is set down plainly in the short pages between the chapters. It describes averages. The two people in this book are not averages, and they swap places more than once.
The story of Manly and Rogers is true. They walked out of Death Valley in the winter of 1849 and they walked back in. Juno, Abe, Kit and Lyle are invented. So is the room. Or I think it is.
Chew Z
I. THE SIGN
1. Juno — Baker, Under the Thermometer

The thermometer in Baker, a gas-stop town on the freeway between Los Angeles and Las Vegas, is a hundred and thirty-four feet tall. I know that because a sign at its foot tells you, and because I had nothing to do at four in the afternoon except read signs. A hundred and thirty-four feet, for the hottest temperature ever measured on Earth, a hundred and thirty-four degrees, over in Death Valley in 1913. Somebody in this town thought that was worth a monument. Somebody in this town was right. There is nothing else in Baker to be proud of.
That day it read a hundred and three. October. The cooler part of the year.

I had eleven dollars, a quarter tank of gas in a Civic that did not belong to me, and a phone with a cracked screen that I kept face down on the seat so I would not have to look at the little red number on the voicemail icon. The number had been a one for two years. It was not going to change. That was the thing about it.

The Civic belonged to a man in Lancaster who had stopped paying for it. I had taken it off his driveway at three in the morning, which is my job, and then instead of taking it to the yard I had kept driving east, which is not my job. I could not tell you why. The road went east. I went with it.

There was a truck parked at the far end of the lot, away from the pumps, a white Ford with a camper shell and a hundred and fifty thousand miles of desert on it. The back window of the shell was open a crack. Through the crack I could see water jugs. A lot of them. Blue five-gallon jugs stacked like bricks, and a box of something, and a rolled-up map.
People who carry that much water carry cash. That is not a fact. That is a feeling I have learned to trust.

I walked over the way you walk over to anything that is not yours, which is slowly and like it is. I put two fingers in the crack of the window and lifted, and it came up easy, and I leaned in, and a voice from the front of the truck said, “There’s a cooler on the left. The beer’s warm. The cash is in my boot.”
I did not jump. I want that on the record. I have been caught by worse.

I stood up. A man was sitting in the cab with the door open on the far side, eating sunflower seeds out of a paper bag. He spat a shell into his palm. He was maybe fifty. Shaved head, gray at the sides where it had been allowed to grow back. A face like something left out in the weather on purpose. Forearms like rope that had been soaked and dried and soaked again.
“Outstanding,” he said. “Broad daylight. Respect.”
“I was looking for a bathroom,” I said.
“In my camper.”
“It’s a big camper.”
He laughed. It was a short laugh, one breath, like a door shutting. “You can have the beer,” he said. “It’s terrible. I bought it as a punishment.”
“For what.”
“I haven’t decided yet.”

I should have walked away. Eleven dollars and a stolen Civic and a man who had seen my face. Any of those is a reason. All three together is a sermon. But he did not reach for a phone, and he did not get out, and he did not do the thing men do when they catch you, which is decide in that second what you owe them. He just kept eating seeds and looking at me like I was weather.
“You’re not calling anybody,” I said.
“No.”
“Why.”
“Because you’re the most interesting thing that’s happened to me in Baker,” he said, “and I’ve been coming through Baker for thirty years.”

That is how it starts. I have thought about it a lot since, and I have tried to make it start somewhere better. It does not. It starts with a man eating sunflower seeds in a hundred and three degrees, and me with my hand in his window, and the thermometer behind us, a hundred and thirty-four feet of somebody’s bad idea, telling the whole desert how hot it was.
2. Abe — Two Go Out

Her name was Juno. She told me that after I gave her a beer, which she drank in four swallows without making a face, which told me a few things. I told her mine, and that I fixed air conditioners in Barstow, which she said was the most useful job a man could have in a desert and the least interesting. She said Abe sounded like a man who builds boats. I said Coldiron sounded like a man who sinks them. She did not laugh. She looked at me like she was filing it.
“Noted,” she said.
We sat on the tailgate. The thermometer said a hundred and two now. It was going down for the night, slowly, the way an old man sits.
I told her what the water was for.

In the winter of 1849, a wagon train going to the gold fields took a shortcut. Shortcuts are how most bad stories in the West begin. The shortcut led them down into a long white valley with mountains on every side, and the wagons could not climb out. Some of the people left on foot and some of them died doing it. Two families stayed, with their children, in a camp by a little spring, because they could not carry the children out and would not leave them.

Two young men went for help. William Lewis Manly and John Rogers. Manly was twenty-nine. Nobody knows how old Rogers was. They walked west, across the mountains and across another desert and another, about two hundred and fifty miles, with almost no food, eating what they could find, until they came down out of the hills to a ranch near what is now Los Angeles. They got food there, and a few horses, and a little one-eyed mule.
“And then they lived happily ever after,” Juno said.
“No.”
“No?”
“That’s the end of the first half,” I said. “I’ll tell you the second half on the second half.”
She looked at the water jugs. She looked at the map. “You’re going to walk it.”
“From the camp by the spring,” I said, “to the ranch. Same line, near as anybody can work out. I’ve got water cached along the way. I drove it last month and buried jugs.”
“That’s two hundred and fifty miles.”
“About.”
“On purpose.”
“It’s the only way I know to do things.”
She drank the last of the beer and looked at the can like it had let her down personally. “So why are you telling me.”
“Because I’ve got a rule,” I said. “Manly had Rogers. Two go out, two come back. I don’t walk it alone. My partner quit yesterday. Called me from a Denny’s in Victorville. Said his wife found out.”
“Found out what.”
“That he was going.”
Juno almost smiled. It went across her face and was gone, like a bird past a window. “And you want me to be Rogers.”
“I want somebody to be Rogers.”
“I stole a car this morning.”
“I figured.”
“I’m not a runner.”
“Nobody’s running. It’s walking. You know how to walk. You walked over here like you owned my truck.”
“I don’t have shoes for it.”

“I’ve got shoes. I’ve got everything. Food, water, salt, a tarp, a first aid kit that could do surgery. I’ll pay you two thousand dollars at the end.” I spat a shell. “And here’s the part you’re going to like. Out there, there’s no phone. No signal for most of it. Nobody comes looking for anybody in Death Valley. Whoever you’re hiding from, they won’t find you, because nobody ever finds anybody out there unless they’re already dead.”

She was quiet for a while. A trucker pulled in and filled up and pulled out. The light went gold and then orange and the thermometer’s numbers went brighter as it got darker, red bulbs against a sky the color of a bruise.
“I’m not hiding from anybody,” she said.
“Then you’ll love it,” I said.
3. Juno — The Lowest Place in America

He drove us in that night. I left the Civic behind the gas station with the keys on the front tire, which is how I would have wanted it done if it was my car, and I did not think about the man in Lancaster again until much later, and then only once.

The road goes down into Death Valley like a road going into a well. You can feel it in your ears. You drive and drive and the land falls away on both sides and the mountains get taller without growing, because it is you that is getting lower. Abe had the window down. The air that came in was warm at ten at night, like the breath of something asleep.
He stopped at a pullout and turned off the engine and the lights, and the dark came down so hard I thought for a second I had gone blind.
“Get out,” he said. “Look up.”

I have lived my whole life in the Central Valley, under a sky the color of a dirty sink. I did not know there were that many stars. I did not know they came in layers, the near ones and the far ones and the far-far ones behind those, like dust on a black floor that went on downward forever. I stood there with my head tipped back and my mouth open and I did not say anything clever, which is rare for me, and Abe did not say anything at all, which I would learn was usual for him.
We slept at Badwater. That is where he wanted to start, the lowest point, though the real camp of 1849 was thirteen miles south. “Start at the bottom,” he said. “It’s the only honest place to start.”

We walked out onto the salt in the dark with headlamps. The ground was white and broken into shapes, six-sided plates the size of tables with ridges between them, like the skin of something huge and dried. It crunched under my feet like old snow. Abe threw down a pad and a sleeping bag and lay on his back in the middle of all that white, and after a while I did the same.

“Up on the cliff behind the parking lot,” he said, “there’s a sign. You’ll see it in the morning. It says SEA LEVEL. It’s way up there. Higher than a building. We’re down here. Two hundred and eighty-two feet under it.”
“That’s a lot of water we’re not under.”
“That’s a lot of everything we’re not under.”

I lay there and the salt ticked and settled under me as it cooled. I thought about the ocean being up there, invisible, a ceiling of nothing three hundred feet thick. I thought about drowning without the water.
“Can I ask you something,” Abe said.
“You can ask.”
“How’d you get the scar on your chin.”
“Boxing.”
“You box?”
“Did. Three years.”
“Why’d you stop?”
“I started winning,” I said.
He thought about that for a while. He did not ask what I meant, and I liked him a little for it.
“Can I ask you something,” I said.
“You can ask.”
“The way you sit. You keep your hand on your chest. Like you’re checking something’s still there.”

He did not answer right away. Then he said, “I died once. Nineteen years ago. Four minutes. Heart just quit. Turned out there’d been a hole in it since I was born and nobody ever noticed, including me.”
The salt ticked. A long way off, something called once and stopped.
“So what was it like,” I said.
“Waiting room,” Abe said. “Bad lighting. Nobody called my name.”
I laughed. I could not help it. It came out of me like something knocked loose. “Same,” I said. “I think they lost my file.”
He turned his head on the pad and looked at me in the starlight for a long time.
“You too,” he said.
“Nine years old,” I said. “Not as long as you. A minute and something. I don’t remember the number.”
“What happened.”
“Hot car.”

He did not say I’m sorry. He did not say anything. He just lay there next to me on the floor of the lowest place in America, and after a while he started to laugh too, not at me, at the whole thing, at the two of us lying there with our two little deaths, and I started again, and we laughed until it hurt, and then we stopped, and it was very quiet, and I fell asleep before I could be embarrassed about it.
4. Abe — The Families
In the morning I showed her the sign.

You have to know where to look. The cliff goes up behind the parking lot, brown and red and broken, and high up on it, small as a postage stamp, there is a white board with black letters. SEA LEVEL. Tourists take pictures of it. They stand on the salt and point up at it, and their faces do something they did not expect. You can see them feel how far down they are.
Juno looked at it a long time.
“Somebody had to climb up there to put that,” she said.
“Somebody did.”
“So they’d know how far down everybody else was.”
“That’s one way of seeing it.”
“What’s the other way.”
“So everybody else would know which way was up.”
She looked at me sideways. “That’s very deep, Abe. Did you get that off a tea bag?”
“Fortune cookie. Panda Express. Barstow.”
“Outstanding,” she said, in my voice, flat, and I did not let her see it hit.

We drove south to the camp. The real one. I parked the truck in the gravel at the edge of it, cracked the windows, and put a note on the dash for the rangers: GONE WALKING. BACK IN FIVE WEEKS. DON’T TOW. There is not much there now. A spring that the books call Bennett’s Well, which is less a well than a place where the ground is a little greener than the ground around it. Some mesquite, a thorny desert tree that grows wherever there is water underground. A sign from the Park Service. The sky. In 1849 this was where two families stayed and waited for twenty-six days with their children in the cold, eating their oxen one at a time, watching the mountain to the west where the two young men had gone over.

I told her about them while I set out the packs. The Bennetts and the Arcans. Asabel Bennett and his wife Sarah, and their three children. Jean-Baptiste Arcan [zhahn bah-TEEST ar-KAHN], a Frenchman, and his wife Abigail and their little boy, Charles. A few men who would not stay and went off on their own and did not all come out. The oxen. One of the oxen was called Old Crump, and he carried children on his back for two hundred miles and came out alive, and they say Bennett swore afterward he would never eat him, and never did.
“That’s the most heartwarming thing you’ve ever said,” Juno said. “It’s about not eating a cow.”
“Ox.”
“Noted.”
She picked up the pack I had set out for her and put it on and adjusted the straps without being shown, which told me something else. She had carried weight before, and not for fun.
“So the two young guys,” she said. “They walk out. They get the food and the one-eyed mule. They come back?”
“That’s the sequel.”
“And?”
“Nobody reads the sequel,” I said.

I said it like a joke and she took it like one. I watched her take it and I felt something I had not felt in a long time, which was ashamed of a joke. It was a true thing dressed up as a joke so that I would not have to say it. I knew the second half of the story. I knew it in my body, the way you know where a stair is in the dark. I was not going to tell her yet.

We stood at the edge of the camp with the packs on. The sun was up over the Black Mountains behind us and the Panamints ahead of us were going from gray to pink. There was no wind. There was no sound at all except a small bird somewhere in the mesquite, saying the same two notes again and again, like somebody trying to remember a phone number.
“Two go out,” Juno said.
“Two come back,” I said.
We walked.
Interlude I — The Sign on the Cliff

Water comes into Death Valley from every side. It runs down off the mountains when it rains, which is almost never. It seeps in underground from a hundred miles away, from springs that were rain ten thousand years ago. A river called the Amargosa [aa-mar-GO-sah] — the word is Spanish for bitter — comes down from Nevada and turns into the valley and gives up there.
None of it ever leaves.

There is no way out downhill. The valley is the bottom of everything around it. Geologists call a place like this a sink, and they mean it the same way you mean the sink in your kitchen, except that this one has no drain. Whatever comes in stays in. The only way out for water is up — to lie on the ground under the sun until it turns to air and rises.

When it goes, it leaves behind what it was carrying. Salt, mostly. Every rain for thousands of years has brought a little salt down into the valley and gone away without it. That is why the floor is white. It is not sand. It is the leftover of every drop that ever arrived and could not leave.
High on the cliff at Badwater, a sign marks where the sea would be if the sea were here. You stand two hundred and eighty-two feet beneath it.
Some places in a person are built the same way. Things flow in. Nothing drains. The only way out is to burn it off, slowly, standing in the heat.
What is left when you do is salt.
II. WALKING OUT
5. Juno — The First Letter
The first thing nobody tells you is that it does not come all at once.

For the first hour, nothing is wrong. My legs were legs. The sun was a sun. We walked up a long gravel fan toward the mountains, the kind of slope that looks flat until you are on it, and I talked. I talked about Bakersfield, which is not a subject. I talked about the tow yard and the man who runs it, Delbert, who has one eyebrow and calls everybody chief. I made a joke about the Park Service sign at the spring, which had a drawing of a covered wagon on it that looked like a loaf of bread on wheels. I was a tourist. I was having a nice time.
Abe walked beside me and answered when he had to. He walked like a man who had made a deal with the ground a long time ago and was keeping his end of it.
The second hour, the body sent me a letter.

It was polite. A small tightness at the back of my left heel, where the new boot rubbed. A dryness at the back of my tongue. Nothing you would stop for. It was the kind of letter that says just so you know. I read it and put it in my pocket and kept walking.
By the third hour I had stopped talking. Not because anything hurt. Because I had run out of things to say, and when I ran out, there was nothing there to take their place.
That was what got me. Not the heat. Not the slope. The quiet.

You do not understand how loud your life is until you take the noise out of it. In Bakersfield there is always something. The tow truck radio. The freeway. A television through a wall. Somebody’s dog. Your own phone buzzing on the seat, face down, the little red number under the glass. Even at three in the morning, hooking up some poor guy’s Kia in the dark, there is the hum of the streetlights and the clank of the chain and the voice in your ear going come on, come on, come on.

Out there, there was nothing. The crunch of our boots. My breathing. A little wind that came and went like something sniffing at us. And under all of it, getting louder as everything else got quieter, the inside of my own head.
It is a terrible neighborhood, my head. I have avoided it for years.

My body was fine. That was the joke. My body was better than fine. Three years of boxing and six years of hauling chains had made me into something that could walk all day and barely notice. By noon Abe was sweating through his shirt and I was barely damp. My legs were bored. They kept going like they had somewhere better to be.
It was everything above my neck that wanted to leave.
At the lunch stop, under the overhang of a boulder the size of a house, Abe handed me a bag of salted almonds and watched me eat.
“You’re quiet,” he said.
“There’s nothing to look at.”
“There’s everything to look at.”
“There’s rocks.”
“That’s what I said.”

I ate the almonds. I could hear myself chewing. I could hear my blood. I thought, very clearly, the way you think something on a staircase in the dark: I could just walk back down. I could walk back down to the truck and take it and be in Vegas by dinner.
I did not say that. I said, “How far today.”
“Eighteen miles.”
“Noted,” I said, and stood up first, so he would not see how much I wanted to sit there forever.
Interlude Ii — The Coward in the Tower
A hundred years ago, a scientist in England named Archibald Hill had men run until they stopped. He wanted to know what made them stop.
He thought it would be the muscles — that they would simply run out, the way a car runs out of gas.
It was not quite that. The muscles still had something left. The men stopped anyway.

Seventy-some years later, a doctor in South Africa named Tim Noakes took the idea further. He said the brain has a watchman. The watchman sits up in a tower and watches the body — the heat, the heart, the fuel, the water — and long before anything is in real danger, he starts shouting. Stop. Stop. You’re going to die. He makes your legs feel like stone. He makes the next step feel impossible. Not because it is.
Because he would rather you stopped a mile too early than a foot too late.

Other scientists have argued with the details ever since. Nobody argues with the shape of it. Most people, when they quit, have a great deal left in them. They never find out how much, because the watchman is very convincing, and he has had their whole life to practice.
He is not your enemy. That is the strange part. He is the oldest friend you have. He kept every one of your ancestors alive long enough to have children, and he has never once been thanked.
He is just a coward who loves you.
6. Abe — Where I Live
There is a place I go.

I do not know what to call it. I have heard people call it the pain cave, which sounds like something you would sell to children at a fair. I have heard a Navy man call it the forty percent, as in, when your mind tells you you are done, you are only forty percent done. I like that one better. It has a number in it. I trust numbers.
But mostly I do not call it anything. I just go there.

It usually starts around mile thirty of a long day. On this walk it started around mile sixty, on the third afternoon, on the long climb out of Panamint Valley, the next valley west of Death Valley, toward the pass. The valley behind us was another white floor, smaller than Death Valley and meaner. Ahead of us the road went up in switchbacks and the sun sat on my neck like a hand.
Here is what it is like, if you have never been.

First the world gets smaller. You stop seeing the mountains. You stop seeing the sky. You see the next ten feet of ground and nothing else, and the ten feet keep arriving and you keep stepping on them. Then the noise starts. Not out loud. Inside. It is the noise of every part of your body filing a complaint at once, and the complaints all come to the same desk, which is you.
Most people, this is where they leave. I understand it. It is a terrible desk to sit at.

But I have been sitting at it for thirty years, and I know something about it that most people do not. If you sit there long enough, the complaints start to repeat. The knee says what it said an hour ago. The feet say what they said yesterday. Nothing new is arriving. It is the same mail, again and again. And once you notice that, you can stop opening it.
That is when I hear the other voice. The one I hired.

I hired him at boot camp in San Diego when I was eighteen. He was a drill instructor named Staff Sergeant Oliver, and he had a voice like a shovel going into gravel, and for thirteen weeks he lived in my ear. When I left the recruit depot I took him with me. I never fired him. I never paid him either. He just stayed.

Is that all you got, Coldiron? Is that the whole show? Your knee hurts? Outstanding. Write it a letter. Your feet hurt? Fantastic. Your feet are not the boss of you. Your heart’s doing the thing? Your heart’s been doing the thing for nineteen years and it hasn’t killed you yet, it’s not going to start on a Tuesday.
It was Thursday. Oliver was never good with days.
I could hear Juno behind me. Her breathing was easy. Her stride was easy. She had not said a word in an hour and I knew it was not her legs.
“You good?” I said over my shoulder.
“Never better,” she said. “This is my favorite mountain.”
“You’ve never been on a mountain.”
“That’s why it’s my favorite.”

At the top of the pass I stopped and turned around. Panamint Valley lay behind us like a dropped plate. Beyond it, the line of mountains we had come over, and somewhere beyond those, low and white and invisible, the floor where we had started.
My heart was going too fast. I could feel it in my throat. I put my hand on my chest, the way she had noticed, and I waited, and Oliver said in my ear, What are you waiting for, Coldiron? A parade?

I wanted to sit down. I wanted to sit down more than I have ever wanted anything. That is the thing about the place I go. It never gets easy. It just gets familiar. I know where the furniture is. I know which stair creaks.
There is one more thing I do down there, and I have never told anybody, because it sounds like something off a poster in a dentist’s office.
I keep a jar.

Not a real one. A jar in my head, on a shelf, with a lid. In it is every hard thing I ever came through. Boot camp in San Diego in August. The hill outside Pristina [PRISH-tee-nah], in Kosovo [KOH-soh-voh], in 1999, with Hendricks on my back, his blood running warm down the inside of my collar. Badwater the first time — the race, a hundred and thirty-five miles from the bottom of Death Valley up to

Whitney Portal, a trailhead high on the side of Mount Whitney — when I threw up at mile ninety and finished anyway, on my hands for the last few yards up the hill to the line. The night in Ridgecrest, the nearest hospital town to the Panamints, when I woke up with a tube in my throat and a nurse telling me I had been dead and was not anymore.

When the desk is full and the mail is all bad, I take the lid off the jar and take one out. I do not live it over. I just look at it. I hold it up to the light. I look at the man in it, the man on his hands on the hill at Whitney Portal, and I say to him, You did that. That was you. This is smaller than that.
It works. I do not know why it works. It works every time.

And then, when I have put the lid back on, I do the other thing. I look forward. Not at the next ten feet. All the way. I make myself see the finish. On this walk, it was always the same picture: the last ridge, and the green valley below, and the cattle, the way Manly saw it. I could see the grass. I could smell it. I could feel what my legs would feel when they stopped.
Jar behind. Valley ahead. You stand in the middle of the two and you walk.

What I did not know yet, on that pass, was that the valley would be a parking lot. And that the jar had a thing in it I never took out, wrapped up at the bottom, a thing I had been walking past every day for nineteen years without once lifting the lid.
I live there. Some men have a cabin by a lake. I have this.
“Outstanding,” I said, out loud, to nobody, and I started down the other side.
7. Juno — The Shade Seller
I met him on the fourth day.

I want to be careful how I say this, because I know how it sounds. I did not see anybody. I did not hear a voice out loud. But somewhere in the middle of the morning, walking across a flat between two ranges with the sun already hot and nothing to look at but Abe’s back and the ground, a voice started talking in my head, and it was not mine.
It was nicer than mine. That was how I knew.
You know you don’t have to do this, it said.
It said it like a friend. Like the friend you have at two in the morning, the one who agrees with you about everybody.

He’s not paying you enough. Two thousand dollars for two hundred and fifty miles? That’s eight dollars a mile. That’s less than you make towing. You could be in Vegas. You could be in a pool. Do you remember pools?

I did remember pools. There was one at a motel in Delano when I was ten, at a foster placement that lasted six weeks, and I swam in it every day until my eyes were pink, and it was the happiest six weeks of my childhood, and I had not thought about it in seventeen years.
There’s shade up ahead, the voice said. See that rock? Just sit down for a minute. He’ll understand. He’s an old man. He wants to sit down too. You’d be doing him a favor.
I looked. There was a rock up ahead, with a scoop of shade under it the color of cold coffee. It looked like a living room. It looked like the best place I had ever seen.

You’re smart, the voice said. Smarter than him. He’s doing this because something’s wrong with him. You can see it. Look at him. He keeps grabbing his chest. He’s going to die out here and you’re going to have to carry him and you don’t even like him.
“I like him fine,” I said out loud.
Abe did not turn around. He did not slow down. He said, “Who are you talking to?”
“Nobody.”
“Tell him I said hi.”
I laughed, and the voice stopped for a second, like somebody interrupted.

Then it came back. It always comes back. It is very patient. It does not get angry. It has a thousand reasons and every one of them is good. That was the worst part. It was not lying. Everything it said was true. The money was bad. The old man was sick. The shade was right there. My feet did hurt now, a little. It was not offering me anything evil. It was offering me a chair.

I started calling it the Shade Seller. I do not know where the name came from. It was just what it was. A man on the side of the road with a cart full of shade, selling it cheap. Real shade. Good shade. And the only price was that you stop walking.

We passed the rock. I did not sit down. The Shade Seller did not seem to mind. He walked along beside me for the rest of the day, pointing things out. There’s a nice one. Oh, look at that one. You’d fit under there.
That night, at the camp, Abe was taping his feet by headlamp and I said, “Do you have one?”
“One what.”
“A voice. That tells you to quit.”
He did not look up from his feet. “Everybody’s got one.”
“What’s yours sound like?”
He thought about it. “Like my mother,” he said. “God rest her. She was a very reasonable woman.”
“Mine sounds like a guy selling shade.”
Abe stopped taping. He looked up at me, and the headlamp put a white circle on my chest, and he looked at me for a long time.
“That’s good,” he said. “That’s a good name for him. Most people never give him a name. They think he’s them.”
Interlude Iii — Why Leaving Feels So Good
In the 1930s, a young scientist at Harvard named B. F. Skinner built a box. Scientists after him used boxes like it to study a simple question.
They put a rat in one. The floor of the box could give a small electric shock, and on the wall was a lever. When the rat pressed the lever, the shock stopped.

The rat learned to press the lever very quickly. That was not surprising. What the scientists noticed was how hard it learned it. The relief of the shock stopping taught the rat fast, and it taught it deep. Relief, it turned out, is one of the strongest teachers there is.

People are the same. Every time you leave a hard place, the mind gets a little reward. The pain stops. The fear stops. The awful conversation ends. And the mind writes it down: this worked. Do it again. The next time, it is easier to leave. And easier. Until leaving is not something you decide. It is something your feet do before you have noticed.
This is how most people build a soft life. Not with one big choice. With a thousand small reliefs, each one sweet, each one teaching the lesson again.
The Shade Seller does not need to lie to you. He does not need to threaten you. He only needs you to remember how good the shade felt the last time.
8. Abe — The Heart Thing
The fifth night I woke at two in the morning and my heart was going like a dropped washing machine.

I know the feeling. I have known it for nineteen years. The doctors call it atrial fibrillation, which means the top part of the heart has stopped beating and started shivering instead, and the bottom part is trying to keep up with a shivering it cannot understand. It is not supposed to kill you, mostly. It is supposed to make you sit very still and think about your choices.
I sat very still. I counted. One, two, a gap, three four five, a gap, six. Like a man falling down stairs.

There is a pill I am supposed to take. I had it. I took it. Then I sat with my back against a rock and my hand flat on my chest and looked up at the stars, which in that part of the desert come down so low you could knock them over with a broom, and I waited for it to sort itself out.
I did not hear her get up. Juno moves like a cat, or a car thief. She was just there, sitting on her heels on the gravel a few feet away, her sleeping bag around her shoulders like a cape.
“What’s going on,” she said.
“Nothing.”
“Your face is gray.”
“It’s the starlight. Everybody’s gray in starlight. You’re gray.”
“Abe.”
“It’s a heart thing. It’s an old heart thing. It does this. It’ll stop.”

She did not say anything. She looked at my hand on my chest and then she looked at my face and then she reached out and put two fingers on the inside of my wrist, cool, like a nurse, and I let her, because I did not know what else to do.
She held them there a long time. Her lips moved. She was counting too.
“That’s not a heartbeat,” she said. “That’s a drum solo.”
I laughed. It hurt a little. “Outstanding,” I said. “A critic.”
She did not laugh.

That frightened me more than my heart did. Juno laughed at everything. I had watched her laugh at a scorpion that tried to get into her boot. I had watched her laugh at her own blister. She had laughed at my death, on the salt, the first night, and I had loved her a little for it. Now she was sitting in the dark with her fingers on my wrist and her face completely still, and she was not laughing, and I understood that whatever she saw on my face was worse than I thought it was.
After a while the stairs stopped falling. One, two, three, four. Steady. Boring. The best sound in the world.
She took her fingers away.
“How many times has it done that,” she said.
“Out here?”
“Out here.”
“Twice.”
“You were going to tell me when?”
“I wasn’t.”
She looked at me. Then she looked away, out at the dark, at the line of mountains we had come over, black against the black.
“You’re an idiot,” she said quietly. “You know that? You’re a giant gray idiot.”
“I’ve been told.”
“By who?”
“Everybody,” I said. “But you’re the first one who took my pulse first.”
9. Juno — Pictures of Water
On the sixth day I saw a lake.
We had come down out of the mountains into another valley, a wide flat one, with a dry lakebed in the bottom of it, white as paper, and on the far edge of it a town with smokestacks that Abe said was

Trona, where they dig salt and soda and borax out of the old lake and the whole place smells like a swimming pool somebody set on fire. We were walking along the edge of the lakebed. It was noon. Nothing moved.
And out on the white there was water.

It was blue. Real blue, deep blue, the blue of a picture in a dentist’s office. It lay out there across the whole flat, shining, with little ripples on it, and the mountains on the far side stood in it upside down. I stopped walking. I could not help it.
“Mirage,” Abe said, behind me.
“I know it’s a mirage.”
“Just saying.”
“I know.”

I knew. I had seen them on the freeway, the wet look on hot asphalt that always goes away when you get there. This was the same thing, only bigger. Only a whole lake. I knew it was not there. I could feel it not being there. And I could not stop looking at it.
Then I saw the car.

It was parked at the edge of the water. A tan Buick, an old one, with a dent in the back door and a coat hanger for an antenna. I knew that car. I knew every inch of that car. I had been inside it with the windows up in August.
The Shade Seller did not say anything. He did not have to. He just showed it to me.
I started walking toward it.

I heard Abe say my name. I heard it the way you hear somebody call you from another room. I was walking out onto the lakebed, and the crust was breaking under my boots, and the car was right there, a quarter mile, less, the sun shining on the windshield so I could not see who was inside, and I thought, if I get there, if I just get there, I can open the door, I can open the door this time.

I walked for a long time. The car did not get closer. That is the thing about pictures of water. They are always the same distance away. You can walk toward them all day and they will keep their exact distance, polite, patient, like something that loves you and will not let you touch it.

Then the light changed. A little cloud, the only one in the sky, went over the sun. And the lake was gone, and the car was gone, and I was standing a mile out on a dry white lakebed by myself with my shadow under me like a hole.

When I turned around, Abe was standing at the edge of the flat where I had left him. He had not followed me. He had not called again. He was just standing there with his hands on his pack straps, waiting, small as a fence post.
I walked back. It took a long time. When I got there he handed me a water bottle without a word and I drank half of it.
“What was it,” he said.
“A lake,” I said.
He nodded. He did not believe me. He did not push.
We walked on. The Shade Seller was quiet for the rest of the afternoon. I think he was pleased with himself.
Interlude Iv — The Sky on the Ground
A desert mirage is not a trick of the mind. It is real. You can photograph it.

Here is how it works. On a hot day, the ground heats the air just above it until that thin layer is much hotter than the air higher up. Light travels a little differently through hot air than through cool air, and when light from the sky comes down at a low angle and hits that hot layer, it bends. It curves back upward, toward your eye.

So when you look out across a hot flat and see water, what you are actually seeing is the sky. A piece of blue sky, bent by the heat and laid down on the ground, shining. It even ripples, because the hot air ripples. Your brain has only ever seen blue shining on the ground one way before, and so it tells you, with total confidence: water.
The mind does the same thing from the inside.

When it wants you out of a hard place, it does not always argue. Sometimes it shows you a picture. A pain that has not happened yet — the body warning of damage long before damage arrives. A memory you have kept locked for years, suddenly so clear you could walk into it. A very good reason to stop, perfectly lit.
None of it is quite a lie. Every picture is made of something real. The sky is real. The memory is real. The pain is real enough.
But every picture of water is a piece of sky, lying on the ground where it does not belong.
10. Abe — Nobody Asked
The cache at mile one hundred and twelve was gone.

I had buried it a month before at the foot of a cut bank, under rocks, six blue jugs and a box of food. I had marked it on the map and taken a picture of it with a Polaroid camera because I do not trust phones. The rocks were there. The hole was there. The jugs were not.
There were tire tracks. Somebody had driven right up.
Juno stood looking down into the hole like it was a grave. “Somebody stole our water,” she said.
“Looks like.”
“Who steals water in the desert?”
“Somebody thirsty.”
“Somebody who drives a truck.”
“Maybe a thirsty truck.”
She turned on me. “This isn’t funny.”
“It’s a little funny.”
We had about a liter and a half between us. The next cache was twenty-two miles on. It was a hundred and one degrees. I knew those numbers and so did she, and we both knew what they added up to.

There was a road two miles south. Not much of one, but a road, and on a road in that part of the desert, sooner or later, there is a mine truck or a Park Service truck or some kid from Ridgecrest in a jacked-up Toyota. You could flag one down. You could get water. You could get a ride.
I said we would walk to the next cache.
“No,” Juno said.
“We’ll go slow. Walk at night. Twenty-two miles. We’ll make it by morning.”
“On a liter and a half.”
“On a liter and a half.”
“With your heart doing the drum solo.”
“My heart’s fine.”

“Your heart was not fine the other night, Abe, I had my fingers on it, it was doing jazz. There’s a road two miles that way. We walk to the road. We wave at a truck. They give us water. We say thank you. We are grownups.”
“No.”
“Why?”

I did not have a good answer. I had a true one. It was the same true answer I have had all my life, and I have never once said it out loud, because it does not sound like anything when you say it out loud. It sounds like a child’s reason. Because I don’t ask.
“Manly and Rogers didn’t have a road,” I said.
“Manly and Rogers didn’t have a road. Abe. They didn’t have roads. It was 1849. They didn’t have antibiotics. You want to give up antibiotics? You want to fight a bear?”
“There’s no bears out here.”
“I’ll find you a bear.”
“You stole a Honda,” I said.
She stopped. Her mouth opened.
“That’s what this is about,” she said. “That’s your argument. I’m a car thief, so you get to die of thirst.”
“I’m saying you’re not the one to lecture me about doing things the right way.”
“I’m not lecturing you about the right way, I’m lecturing you about the alive way.”
“Same thing.”
“It is not the same thing! The right way is your stupid rule! The alive way is a guy in a truck with a gallon of Arrowhead!”

We were standing in the full sun, screaming at each other next to an empty hole, two dead people with a liter and a half of water. A raven came down and landed on a rock about thirty feet off and watched us with its head on one side like a man at a tennis match.
Juno saw it. She pointed at it.
“Even he thinks you’re an idiot,” she said.
The raven said something hoarse and rude.
“See?” she said. “He agrees with me.”

And I started to laugh. I could not stop it. It came up out of me from somewhere under the ribs, the place the heart thing lives, and it bent me over. Juno stared at me with her fists still clenched, and then her face cracked too, and she was laughing, and she sat down hard in the gravel and laughed, and I sat down next to her, and the raven watched the two of us howl beside the grave of our water, and after a while it lost interest and flew away.
When we were done we sat there breathing.
“We’re walking to the cache,” Juno said. “Aren’t we.”
“Yes.”
“Tonight.”
“Yes.”
“You’re a stubborn gray idiot.”
“Yes.”
She wiped her eyes. “Noted,” she said.

We walked all night on a liter and a half. It was the worst night of my life, and I have had some. We got to the cache at six in the morning and the jugs were there, all six, and I have never in my life seen anything as beautiful as a plastic jug with water in it, not the ocean, not a woman, not the stars. Juno drank until she was sick and then drank again.
Then we sat on the cut bank in the first sun with the jugs between our knees and something happened that I have never been able to explain to anybody who has not done a hard thing on purpose.
We were happy.

Not relieved. Relief is the shade closing over you. This was something else. It came up out of the ground through the seat of my pants. It was in my hands and my feet and behind my eyes. The sun came over the mountains and lit the whole flat gold, and every rock had a shadow, and every shadow was sharp, and I could see further than I have ever seen, and everything I could see I had walked through. Juno lay back on the gravel with her arms out like a kid making a snow angel and laughed at the sky for no reason at all.
“What is this,” she said. “What is this.”
“This is what it’s for,” I said.
“This?”
“This. Every bad mile. This is the receipt.”
She lay there a long time with her eyes shut and the sun on her face. “It’s better than drugs,” she said.
“You’d know.”
“I would,” she said. “It is.”

There is a scientific word for it, I am told. The body pours out its own medicine when you have suffered long enough, a thing like the stuff in marijuana, made in your own blood. I do not care what it is called. I have been chasing that morning for thirty years and I will chase it until I die.

Neither of us said anything about the road. But I knew, and she knew, and I think the raven knew, that there had been a hand held out to me on that flat, a very easy one, and that I had not taken it, and that it had nothing to do with Manly and Rogers at all.
III. THE PARKING LOT
11. Juno — Time Goes Wide
Somewhere after the second week the days stopped having edges.

I could not tell you which day we crossed the long valley with the dry lake and the railroad. I could not tell you which night we slept in the wash with the coyotes going off like a car alarm, or which morning I woke up with a beetle the size of a thumb sitting on my sleeping bag, looking at me with no opinion. They all ran together. One long day with dark patches in it.
And inside the day, time did something I did not know it could do.
It went wide.

I would be walking, counting steps, because counting was the only thing that kept the Shade Seller from getting a word in. One, two, three, up to a hundred, then start again. And somewhere around sixty I would lose the count, and I would look up, and I would have no idea how long I had been walking. A minute. An hour. The sun had not moved. Abe’s back was the same size. A single minute would open up in front of me like a room, and I would walk into it, and I could walk around inside it, and look at the walls, and it would not end.
I thought I was going crazy. Then I thought, no, this is what crazy is for. This is what it is supposed to feel like. Your mind gets so tired of the outside that it starts building rooms.

On the fourteenth night we camped in a wash under a cottonwood that should not have been there, the only tree for ten miles, with a trickle of real water under it that Abe said was a spring nobody had a name for. We had made a fire, which we did not usually, out of dead branches. The firelight came and went on Abe’s face. He was sitting with his hand on his chest again.
I told him.

I do not know why that night. I think it was the minute that would not end. I think I had walked around inside it for so long that I had seen everything in there, and there was only one thing left that I had not looked at, sitting in the corner like a box.
“The hot car,” I said.
He did not say anything. He put a branch on the fire.

“My brother’s name is Kit. He’s five years older. Our mom worked doubles at a cannery and then she didn’t work at all and then there was a guy, and then there wasn’t. Kit raised me. That’s not a figure of speech. He made the sandwiches. He did the forms. He was fourteen.”
The fire popped.

“It was August. He had Mom’s car. He wasn’t old enough to drive and he drove anyway, he drove all the time. He parked outside a Rite Aid. He said, wait here, ten minutes, don’t open the door for anybody. And he went in.”
I could feel my heartbeat in my teeth.

“He didn’t come back. Turned out he got caught. Stealing. Something stupid. A security guy held him in the back. Hours. And I stayed in the car. Because he said wait. And the thing is, Abe — I could have gotten out. The doors opened from the inside. I could have just opened the door and gotten out any time I wanted. I didn’t. Because he said wait, and I wanted to be good. I wanted him to come back and see I’d been good.”
My voice did not sound like mine. It sounded like it was coming from the bottom of a pool.

“A guy walking by saw me. He broke the window with a rock. I was already — I’d stopped. They said I’d stopped. At the hospital they said my heart wasn’t going when the ambulance got there and then it was. A minute and something. I don’t remember the number.”
“Then what,” Abe said. Very quietly.

“Then they took him. Kit. Because he left a nine-year-old in a hot car. Two years in juvenile hall. They took me too. Foster homes. Mom never got either of us back. That was the end of all of us. Because of me. Because I sat in a car like an idiot when I could have just opened the door.”
“Juno.”

“And when I was sixteen he came to find me. He was out by then. He came to the placement in Delano, a different house this time, and stood on the porch. And I wouldn’t see him. I told the lady to tell him I didn’t live there. I watched him from the window. He stood there for twenty minutes and then he left. So I left him. You see? I left him twice. Once in the car. Once on the porch.”
The fire was down to coals. I could not see Abe’s face anymore, only the shape of him, the hand on his chest.

He did not say it wasn’t my fault. He did not say I was a child. He did not say any of the things people say. He just sat there in the dark with me, and let the thing I had said stay in the air between us, and did not try to clean it up.
I have thought about that a lot since. I think it was the kindest thing anyone has ever done for me. Everybody else always tried to take it away from me. He just let me have it.
After a long time he said, “You want the last of the cocoa?”
“Yes,” I said.
He made it. We drank it out of the same cup, taking turns, and neither of us said anything else that night.
Interlude V — The Long Second

A scientist named David Eagleman once wanted to know if time really slows down when you are afraid. Everybody says it does. People in car crashes say the crash took forever. People who fall say they had time to think a hundred things on the way down.

So he built an experiment. He took volunteers to the top of a tall tower at an amusement park, a ride where you fall backward about a hundred feet into a net, with nothing to hold. He strapped a small screen to their wrists that flashed numbers too fast to read at normal speed. If time really slowed down for them as they fell, they would be able to read the numbers.
They could not read the numbers. Time did not slow down.
But afterwards, when he asked them how long the fall had taken, they said it had taken about a third longer than it really had. Every one of them was sure.

Here is what he found. Fear does not slow the clock. It makes the mind write down everything. Every second of a frightening fall is recorded in full, every detail, every color, while an ordinary second is barely recorded at all. And when you look back at a memory that is very full, it feels long.
In the hard place, the clock does not change. You just stop throwing the seconds away.
12. Abe — Out
We came down out of the last canyon on the nineteenth day.

I had been walking toward that place for almost forty years. I mean that. The first time I read Manly’s book, Death Valley in ’49, the story he wrote down as an old man, I was twelve years old, in the Barstow library, which was air conditioned and was therefore the best place in Barstow. I read it twice. I read the part where the two young men come over the last ridge and see the green valley below them, and cattle in it, and they know they are going to live. I read it until the page was soft.
And here it was. The last ridge. The valley.
There were no cattle.
There was a roller coaster.

It came up over the hill in front of us like a spine, red and yellow and blue, a thing of steel loops as tall as a building, and as we stood there a train of little cars went screaming up it and over the top and down, and from a mile away we could hear the people in it. Screaming. Happily. That is the worst kind.
Beyond it there were more. Towers and loops and drops, and a flagpole, and a parking lot the size of a small country, and in the parking lot, shining in the sun, a great many cars.

I took the map out of my pocket and looked at it. I had known. I had known for years. Rancho San Francisco [RAHN-cho san fran-SIS-ko], the cattle ranch where Manly and Rogers came down to food and life, is under a theme park now, or near enough. I had seen it from the freeway. But I had never come at it from the other way, out of the desert, on foot, after two hundred and fifty miles. I had never seen it the way they saw it.
“Abe,” Juno said. “Is that—”
“Yes.”
“We walked out of Death Valley—”
“Yes.”
“—for three weeks—”
“Nineteen days.”
“—to get to Magic Mountain?”
I did not say anything. The roller coaster went over the top again. The people screamed.

Juno started to laugh. Not her usual laugh. Something bigger, from further down. She bent over with her hands on her knees and laughed until she could not breathe, and then she straightened up and looked at the roller coaster and started again. I tried to keep my face straight. I lasted about four seconds. Then I was laughing too, standing there on the last ridge of the Manly route with two hundred and fifty miles of salt in my socks, laughing at the most beautiful and stupid thing I had ever seen.

We walked down to it. We walked across the parking lot. People looked at us. I did not blame them. We looked like something that had been dug up. A little boy in a Batman shirt stared at Juno with his mouth open, and she leaned down and said, very seriously, “Don’t ride the big one. It’s not worth it.”

And under all of it, under the laughing and the tiredness and the shame of how we smelled, I felt it again, the thing from the morning at the cache. It came up through the soles of my boots off the hot black asphalt of the Magic Mountain parking lot. Two hundred and fifty miles. Every step of it in my legs. I looked at Juno and I could see it in her too, in her face, under the dirt. She did not have a word for it. I did not give her one. Some things you should be allowed to find out for yourself.
At the edge of the lot, there was a curb in the shade of a pepper tree. We sat down on it.
That was it. That was the end of the first half.

Juno laughed again, quietly, and then the laugh turned into something else, and she put her face in her hands and was sick into the ivy behind the curb, very neatly, and sat back up and wiped her mouth.
“Sorry,” she said.
“Don’t be.”
“I think I’m just tired.”
“You’re just done,” I said. “It does that. When you stop, everything you didn’t let yourself feel comes in all at once. It’s like opening a closet.”
She looked at me. “You’re sitting very still.”
“I’m resting.”
“You’ve got your hand on your chest again.”
I took it away. I put it on my knee.
She did not say anything. Neither did I. Behind us the roller coaster went over the top and the people screamed, again and again, like something being born.
13. Juno — The Easy Door
Abe got us a motel with a pool in Valencia, the town that has grown up around the theme park.

He did it without asking. He just walked up to the desk looking like something the desert spat out and put a card down and came back with two keys. Two rooms. Next to each other. He handed me mine and then he handed me an envelope.
“Two thousand,” he said. “I said I’d pay you at the end.”
I looked at the envelope. “This is the end?”
“This is the end of what I asked you for,” he said. “You walked out. Two went out. Deal’s done.”
He went into his room and shut the door.

I stood in the parking lot of the motel with the envelope in my hand. It was the most money I had held at one time in my life. I could feel it through the paper, the thickness of it. It felt like a door.
The pool was blue. Real blue. The blue of a picture in a dentist’s office. It did not go away when I walked toward it.

I took off my boots and my socks, which had become something else, a kind of leather, and I sat on the edge of the pool with my feet in the water. My feet were white and swollen and the skin on the bottoms had gone strange, like the skin on old milk. The water was cold. I sat there and cried a little bit, without making any noise, because my feet were in a swimming pool and nothing hurt.
The Shade Seller sat down next to me.

He did not need to say much. Here it is, he said. Here’s the shade. You earned it. There’s a bus station in Santa Clarita. There’s a bus to Vegas at eight. Two thousand dollars in Vegas. A pool every day. You walked two hundred and fifty miles. You’re the toughest person you know. You don’t owe anybody anything.
All true. Every word of it.

I took out my phone. I had turned it off on the first day and had not turned it on since. I turned it on. It took a long time to find a signal and then it found one, and it buzzed, and buzzed again, and there were texts from Delbert at the yard, and there were missed calls from numbers I did not know, and there in the corner, the little red number. One.
Two years.
I pressed it. I held the phone to my ear.
There is a little click when a voicemail starts, and then a breath. Before the words. Somebody breathing in, getting ready.
I heard Kit breathe in.
I pressed stop.

I sat there with the phone in my lap and my feet in the pool, and my heart was going so hard I thought I might go into the water. I sat there until the sun went down and the pool lights came on, underwater, green and blue, and the water glowed like something alive.
Then I heard Abe’s door open.
Interlude Vi — Two Kinds of Hard
Scientists who study how men and women meet pain and effort have found real differences, on average. They are worth knowing. They are also only averages, and every person is a mix.

In long, steady efforts — hours, not seconds — women’s muscles tend to tire more slowly than men’s. The longer the race, the closer women come to men. In 2002 and again in 2003, a woman named Pam Reed won the Badwater race outright, a hundred and thirty-five miles from the bottom of Death Valley to the side of Mount Whitney, in July, ahead of every man. Other women have since won some of the hardest races on earth, outright, against everybody.

In the mind, the differences run the other way. When something hurts, women more often turn it over and over, thinking about it, talking about it, reaching for other people. Men more often push the feeling down, keep quiet, and carry it alone. Research finds that men ask for help far less than women do, even when the help might save their lives. One old study found that men will hold their hand in ice water longer when a woman is in the room watching.
Each way of being hard has a soft place hidden in it. The one who goes over and over the pain can get lost in it. The one who pushes it down can carry it until it breaks him.
And each person, somewhere, has the other’s skill — unused, waiting, like a tool in a drawer they have never opened.
14. Abe — The Sequel
I came out of my room and sat down on the plastic chair next to the pool, beside where she was sitting with her feet in the water. The pool light made her look like something drowned and come back.
“You going to Vegas?” I said.
“How’d you know?”
“Everybody goes to Vegas from here. It’s the law.”
She did not say anything.

I had been sitting on the edge of the motel bed for two hours with the curtains shut. My heart had been doing the thing on and off since the roller coaster. I had taken the pill. I had sat there in the dark trying to think of a way to say it that did not sound like a beggar, and there was not one, so I came out to say it like a beggar.
“I’m going to tell you the second half,” I said.
She looked at me.

“Manly and Rogers got to the ranch. They got food. They got a few horses and a little one-eyed mule. They could have stayed. Nobody would have blamed them. They were twenty-something and half dead and they had just walked across hell. There was a whole state of California to go and be rich in.”
“But they went back.”

“They went back. The whole way. Over the same mountains. The horses died on the way. The mule didn’t. That little one-eyed mule climbed rock a goat wouldn’t. Twenty-six days after they left, they walked back into the camp by the spring. Most of the people who’d been waiting had given up and left. But the two families were still there. They’d been sitting there for almost a month, watching the mountain, eating their oxen, sure the two boys were dead. When Manly fired his gun to let them know, a man came out from under a wagon and threw his arms up and shouted, The boys have come! The boys have come!”
I stopped. I had not meant to stop. My voice had done something.

“Then they all walked out together,” I said. “And when they got to the top of the last mountain, somebody looked back down at the valley and said, Goodbye, Death Valley. That’s where the name comes from. It’s a goodbye.”
Juno did not say anything for a long time. The pool filter hummed.
“That’s not why you’re doing this,” she said. “Is it. It’s not for the history.”
“No.”
“Who’s Lyle?”
I looked at her.
“You talk in your sleep,” she said. “Every night. You say Lyle and you say I’m coming. Every night, Abe.”
So I told her.

Nineteen years ago I did this walk with a man named Lyle Pruitt. We had been in the Marines together. He was the only friend I ever had who could keep up with me and the only one who could make me laugh while doing it. We started at the spring, at the camp, the same as she and I had. Same route. Two go out.
On the third day, in a side canyon in the Panamints, Lyle stepped on a loose rock and broke his ankle. It was bad. The bone was wrong. He could not walk.

We had a choice and I made it. I left him in the shade of a cliff with most of the water and went for help. There was a dirt road eleven miles east. I said I’d be back by morning with a truck. I’ll be back by morning. Those were the words.
Seven miles from the road, my heart stopped.

I do not remember it. I remember the ground coming up. I remember a feeling like a door closing in another room. Then I remember the waiting room, the bad light, the carpet. Nobody called my name. And then I remember a hospital ceiling in Ridgecrest, three days later.

A man in a Jeep had found me. A rockhound, looking for quartz. He did CPR on me in the gravel for four minutes until my heart came back. Then he put me in the Jeep and drove. I was out for three days. When I woke up I told them about Lyle. I told them where he was. They sent a helicopter.
He had been there four days. He was sitting up against the cliff where I left him. The water was gone. He had written something on the rock beside him with a stone, and it said ABE COMING.

“So I didn’t come,” I said. “I walked out and I didn’t walk back in. My heart stopped and that was the reason, and it was a good reason, and he’s dead anyway. Nineteen years. I’ve done Badwater eleven times. I’ve done every hard thing I could find. None of it was the right one.”
Juno’s feet moved in the pool. Little circles.
“So you want to walk back in,” she said. “To the camp.”
“The whole way.”
“With your heart doing the drum solo.”
“Yes.”
“And you need two.”
“Two go out,” I said. “Two come back.”
She looked at me for a long time. Then she said, “Are you asking me?”

And I could not do it. I sat there with my mouth open and the words right there behind my teeth, and I could not get them out. Will you come with me. Four words. I have carried a man down a hill in Kosovo. I have walked a hundred and thirty-five miles through a hundred and twenty degrees eleven times. I could not say four words to a car thief by a motel pool.
“I’m telling you the second half,” I said. “That’s all.”
She looked at me a while longer. Then she nodded, slowly, like somebody deciding not to say something.
“Noted,” she said.
IV. WALKING BACK IN
15. Juno — Noted
I did not go to Vegas.

I would like to tell you there was a moment. A light from above, a decision. There was not. I sat by the pool until the pool lights went off at eleven, and then I went to my room and lay on the bed in my clothes and did not sleep, and in the morning I went and knocked on Abe’s door.
He opened it. He looked like he had not slept either. He had his boots on.
“I’m coming,” I said.

He did not say thank you. He did not say why. He looked at me for a second with his face doing nothing, and then he nodded once, and stepped back to let me in, and that was how I knew he was saying thank you. Abe says everything important by not saying it. It is the most annoying thing about him and I would not change it.
“For the money,” I said. “I want another two thousand.”
“Done.”
“And I want a better pack. Mine pulls on the left.”
“Done.”
“And I want to know why you bought a deer cart.”

It was leaning in the corner of his room. Two big wheels, an aluminum frame, a pair of handles like a wheelbarrow, and straps. I had seen them in sporting goods stores. Hunters use them to drag a dead deer out of the woods.
“For the water,” Abe said. “The caches are spent. We drank them on the way out.” He looked at the cart. “We need a mule.”
“That’s not a mule. That’s a stretcher with wheels.”
“Manly had a one-eyed mule.”
“Manly had a mule.”
“Then it’s a one-eyed mule,” Abe said, and he took a black marker out of his pocket and drew an eye on the left side of the frame. One eye. It looked surprised.
I looked at it for a long time.
“I hate that I love it,” I said.

We walked out of Valencia that afternoon with twelve gallons of water lashed to the one-eyed mule, and a plan to fill up again in Ridgecrest and Trona, past the parking lot of Magic Mountain, past the roller coasters, back up into the hills the way we had come. The people on the big one were screaming. I did not look back. I knew what it looked like. I knew what all of it looked like now. That was the difference. Going out, everything was new, and new things carry you. Going back, every rock is a rock you already met.

The Shade Seller walked along beside me, quiet for once. I think he was confused. I think he could not understand why anybody would walk back into a place they had just gotten out of. I could not have explained it to him. I could not have explained it to me.
All I knew was that if I got on that bus I would be getting on it for the rest of my life. And I knew that the way you know a stair in the dark.
16. Abe — The Wrong Direction
Walking back in is worse.
Nobody tells you that, either. You would think it would be easier. You know the way. You know where the water is, the shade, the bad rocks. You have done it once.

But going out, there is something pulling you. A finish. A green valley you have read about since you were twelve. Every step brings it nearer, and the nearer it gets, the more it pulls, and you lean into it like a rope.

Going back in, there is nothing pulling. There is only something you are walking toward on purpose, and every step, the body asks you the same question. Why are we going this way? We were out. We got out. Why are we going back?

And you have no answer the body can understand. The body does not understand Lyle. The body does not understand promise. The body understands water and shade and away from the heat. You are asking it to walk back into the oven on purpose, and it is not stupid, and it knows it.
On the fifth day back, in the long valley with the railroad, my heart started doing the thing and did not stop.

Before, it had come and gone. A night, an afternoon. Now it stayed. All day. A falling-down-stairs feeling in my chest that would not end. I took the pill. I took another one. It slowed but it did not stop. I could feel it in my fingertips, a stutter, and in the back of my head, and in my mouth, a taste like pennies.
I did not tell her.

I hid it badly. I knew I was hiding it badly. I walked behind her instead of in front, so she would not see my face. When we stopped I sat with my back to her. When she asked how I was I said outstanding in a voice that was not outstanding at all.

Oliver was in my ear all day. Is that it, Coldiron? A little flutter? You’ve walked through worse. You walked Badwater with a sprained ankle. You walked the Kosovo hills with a man on your back. Your heart wants to quit? Your heart doesn’t vote.
And for the first time in thirty-three years, I heard something underneath Oliver. Another voice. Quieter. Not the Shade Seller. Something I had not heard before.
You could ask her, it said.
That was all. Four words. It did not tell me to stop. It did not tell me to go back. It just said: you could ask.
It frightened me more than my heart did.

That night we camped in the wash under the cottonwood with the spring nobody had named. The same place she had told me about the car. She made the fire this time. I sat with my back against the tree and she sat across from me, and the firelight went back and forth between us.
“How bad,” she said.
“What?”
“Abe.”
I did not answer. She got up and came around the fire and sat on her heels beside me and put her two fingers on my wrist, the way she had that night in the mountains. She held them there.
“It’s been going all day,” she said.
“It’s fine.”
“It’s going like a washing machine full of shoes.”
“It’s fine.”
“There’s a road,” she said. “Four miles. Back the way we came. We can be at a hospital in Ridgecrest by tomorrow.”
“No.”
“Why?”
And I opened my mouth. I opened it to say the same thing I had said at the empty cache, Manly and Rogers didn’t have a road, and it would not come out. What came out was something else.

“Because if I stop now,” I said, “I never go back. I know myself. I go to Ridgecrest and they put me in a bed and I lie there and tell myself I’ll do it next year, and I never do. Like last time. Nineteen years of next year.”
Juno did not say anything. She kept her fingers on my wrist.
“I’m not asking you to stay,” I said.
“I know you’re not,” she said. “That’s the problem.”
Interlude Vii — Laughing in the Dark
People have always made jokes in the worst places on earth.

In the trenches of the First World War, soldiers put out newspapers full of jokes about the mud, the rats, and the generals, printed on a press they had found in the ruins of a town. Doctors and nurses in emergency rooms, firefighters, police — people who spend their working lives beside death — are famous for a kind of humor that would shock anyone who overheard it. Researchers who study them have found it helps. Not to make light of what they see, but to keep them able to look at it at all.

A man named Viktor Frankl, a doctor, spent three years in the death camps of the Second World War. He lost almost everyone he loved there. Afterward he wrote a book about how a person survives the unsurvivable. In it he said something surprising. He said that even in the camps, people joked. He and a friend made a promise to each other to invent one funny story every day, about something that might happen after they were free. He called humor another of the soul’s weapons in the fight for self-preservation.
In the hard place, a joke is not disrespect. It is not denial. It is the mind finding one small handhold on a wall with no handholds, and holding on.
A joke in the dark is a hand on the rope.
17. Juno — The Waiting Room Leaks
On the tenth night back, walking in the dark to save water, we reviewed the afterlife.

It was Abe’s idea, or mine. I cannot remember. We were both so tired that our mouths were doing things without us. His heart was going like shoes in a dryer and he would not talk about it, so we talked about this instead.
“One star,” I said. “No parking.”
“Two stars,” Abe said. “The chairs were bolted together. I respect a chair that’s bolted together. You know where you stand.”
“You don’t stand. You sit. That’s the whole problem. Nobody ever says, Juno Marrow, come on back.”
“The magazines,” Abe said.
“Oh my God, the magazines.”
“There was a Reader’s Digest from before I was born. I read a whole article about a man who was struck by lightning seven times. I thought, this is a message. I didn’t know what it was.”
“I’d leave a comment card,” I said. “But there’s no pen. There’s never a pen.”
“Would not die there again.”
“Would not recommend.”
“Food was terrible.”
“There was no food.”
“That’s what I’m saying.”

We laughed in the dark until he had to stop and put his hands on his knees, and I stood next to him and waited and did not say anything about the sound his breathing made. When he could walk again we walked again. I did not know yet that we were going to be reviewing it in person in a few days. I would like to think that if I had known, I would still have made the joke about the pen.
I probably would have made it twice.
On the eleventh day back we came over the pass and down into Panamint Valley, and the light was wrong.
I want to be careful how I say this, too.

It was evening. The sun had gone down behind the mountains we had just crossed. Normally, in the desert, when the sun goes down, the heat shimmer goes away. The air stops moving. Everything gets sharp and still and blue.
The shimmer did not go away.

It stayed on the valley floor after the sun was down. It hung there in the dusk, a low wavering layer like heat off a road, and under it the ground looked like it was moving. Not water. Not a mirage. Something else. Like the whole valley floor was a picture someone was holding up, and their hands were shaking.
And there was a sound. Very faint. Under the wind. I did not notice it at first. Then I did, and I could not stop noticing it.
A hum. A thin electric hum, like a light that needs a new tube. Like a fluorescent light in a ceiling. In a room.
I stopped walking. Abe stopped behind me with the one-eyed mule.
“Do you hear that,” I said.
He did not say anything. I turned around. He was standing very still, with his head a little on one side, the way the raven had.
“Yeah,” he said.
We stood there. The hum went on. The light shook.

Then I smelled it. That was the worst part. It came on a little breath of wind from down the valley, and it was not a desert smell. It was not creosote, the little greasy bush that covers this desert, or dust or salt. It was carpet. Old carpet, the cheap kind, the thin gray industrial kind they put in offices and clinics and the waiting rooms of places nobody wants to be. Carpet that has been walked on by ten thousand people in bad shoes. Carpet and burnt coffee and that air that has been breathed by too many people and never let out.
I knew that smell. I had smelled it for one minute and something, when I was nine.
“Abe,” I said.
“I know,” he said.
“Is this—”
“I don’t know.”
“It’s the same,” I said. “It’s the same place.”
“I know,” he said again. His voice was very quiet. “Bad lighting.”
“Nobody called my name,” I said.

And we both laughed. I do not know how. We stood on the edge of Panamint Valley at dusk with the waiting room leaking up out of the ground in front of us like steam out of a grate, and we laughed, two dead people, two very small sharp laughs, the way you laugh at a funeral when something goes wrong.
Then the wind changed, and the smell was gone, and the shimmer settled down into the ordinary dark, and the hum stopped, or I stopped hearing it.

We made camp. We did not talk about it. I lay in my sleeping bag and looked at the stars and told myself it was the heat. It was the tiredness, the miles, the not-enough-water. It was a mind that had been walking for thirty days making rooms out of nothing. Everything I told myself was true.
I lay awake for a long time. And when I finally slept, I could still hear it, very faint, under the wind.
18. Abe — Lyle’s Fire
Two nights later we camped at the mouth of the canyon.

I had not told her where we were. I had been walking toward it for two days with my heart falling down the stairs, and I had not said a word. But she knew. She looked up at the cliffs and then at me, and she did not ask.

It is a side canyon off the main one. You would not look at it twice. A gravel floor, a little dry waterfall, cliffs on both sides the color of an old scab. About a mile up, there is a place where the left-hand cliff leans out and makes a long shade in the afternoon. That is where I left him.
I did not go up there. I could not. I sat at the mouth of the canyon with my back to it and ate cold beans out of the can and did not taste them.
Juno sat across from me. She did not make a fire. She did not say anything. She was being kind, which is the hardest thing to watch someone do for you.
When it was full dark, I saw the fire.

It was up the canyon. A mile, maybe. Small. Orange. Flickering against the cliff where the cliff leans out. A little campfire, the size of a man’s two hands, the kind you make with dead creosote when you are cold and alone and waiting for a truck.
I looked at it for a long time.
“Juno,” I said.
She turned. She looked where I was looking. I watched her face. I watched her see it.
“It’s a mirage,” I said. “Heat. Light bending. There’s a word for it.”
“Sure,” she said.
“Or campers.”
“Sure.”
“Nobody camps up there. There’s no reason to.”
“Abe.”
“I know who it is,” I said.

She did not say anything. She reached across the dark and found my hand, and held it, and I let her. It was the first time I had let anybody hold my hand since my mother in the hospital in 1996. Her hand was hard and dry and very strong, and she held on, and we sat there together at the mouth of the canyon and watched the little fire up against the cliff, burning, steady, patient, a mile off, the way a light in a window burns for somebody who is late.
It burned all night. I know because I did not sleep.
In the morning, there was nothing up there. I knew there would not be. I did not go and look.
As we walked away down the wash, Juno said, very quietly, without looking at me, “He kept it going a long time.”
I could not answer her. She did not need me to.
19. Juno — The Camp
We came down into Death Valley on the fifteenth day back.

The sign was still on the cliff at Badwater. SEA LEVEL. You could not see it from out there, but I knew where it was now, a white speck on the brown rock, high, impossibly high, like a note somebody had pinned to the top of the world.
