It was November now, the month the valley is supposed to cool. It had not cooled. It was as hot as the day we left. The floor was white and burning and the shimmer stood up off it all day and, at dusk, did not lie down.

Abe walked behind the mule. He walked very slowly. His lips were gray. He stopped every few hundred yards with his hand flat on his chest and stood there, and I stood there, and the one-eyed mule stood there with its marker eye looking surprised at the mountains, and then he would nod and we would go on.
The hum was back. All day. A thin bright buzz under everything. I could feel it in my fillings.

We came to the spring late in the afternoon. The camp. Bennett’s Well. The place we had started, thirty-five days before, with the little bird in the mesquite saying the same two notes over and over like somebody trying to remember a phone number.
They were there.
I want to say this as simply as I can, because there is no other way to say it.
The families were there.
They were sitting in the shade of the mesquite, the way you would sit in a waiting room. Some on the ground. Some on wooden boxes.

There was a wagon, one, gray, with its cover torn and the ribs showing like an animal’s. There were men in long coats gone the color of dust, and women in bonnets, and children. A little boy with a stick, drawing in the dirt. A girl holding a smaller girl. An ox, huge and patient, lying down with its legs folded under it, chewing nothing, and I knew without being told that his name was Crump.
They were thin. All of them. So thin. And they were patient, so patient, sitting there the way people sit when they have been waiting so long they have forgotten what for.
The light over them was wrong. It was not sunlight. It was the color of fluorescent light, flat and gray-white, coming from nowhere, and it hummed.

A woman in a bonnet looked up as we came in. She had a kind face, worn down to the bone. She looked at Abe, and then at me, and then she smiled, and moved over a little on her box, and patted the space beside her.
There’s shade, she said.
I heard it. I am telling you I heard it. And it was the Shade Seller’s voice. It was his exact voice, coming out of her mouth.
Abe made a sound beside me. Not a word. A sound like something tearing.

There was a man standing at the edge of the shade, away from the others. A young man. Younger than Abe by far. Big through the shoulders, with a Marine haircut grown out a little, in a faded T-shirt, an old field jacket knotted around his waist by the sleeves. One of his boots was unlaced and his ankle was wrapped in a bandage gone brown. He was standing on it. It did not seem to bother him.
He was looking at Abe. He did not look angry. That was the thing. He did not look angry at all. He looked like a man seeing an old friend come in through the door of a bar.
“Hey, Coldiron,” he said.
Abe did not move.
“Took you long enough,” Lyle said, and smiled.
I could not watch it. I looked away.
And that was when I saw her.

She was sitting by herself at the far edge of the camp, apart from the others, where the shade ran out. On the ground, in the dirt, with her knees pulled up. A little girl. Nine years old, maybe. Thin legs. Dirty sneakers, the kind with lights in the heels, but the lights were dead. A T-shirt much too big for her, an adult’s, yellow, with a cartoon on the front faded almost to nothing. Her hair was stuck to her head with sweat.
She was not looking at me. She was looking at her hands. Her fingers. She was holding them up in front of her face, turning them, looking at the nails.
The nails were broken. All of them. Torn down to the quick.
She would not look at me.
I knew that T-shirt. It had been Kit’s.
V. SALT
Interlude Viii — The Memory That Rewrites Itself
For a long time, people thought memory worked like a filing cabinet.
Something happens, the mind writes it down, and the page goes in a
drawer. When you remember, you take the page out and read it. The
page does not change.
It does change.
A scientist named Elizabeth Loftus spent fifty years showing how much.
She found that a single word in a question — smashed instead of hit —
could make people remember a car crash as faster than it was, and
remember broken glass that was never there. Other scientists found
that every time we bring a memory up, the mind rebuilds it, and then
puts the rebuilt version away. Not the original. The new one. Remember
something a hundred times and you have rebuilt it a hundred times, and
each time a little of what you needed it to be gets mixed in.
And there is something stranger. A psychologist named Ronnie
Janoff-Bulman found that people who have been through something
terrible very often blame themselves for it, even when there was
nothing they could have done. It seems cruel. It is not. If it was your
fault, then you had some control. If you had control, then next time you
can stop it. And then the world is not a place where things simply
happen to you while you watch.
Being guilty is terrible. Being helpless is worse.
Sometimes the mind would rather be guilty than helpless. Guilt at least
gives you something to hold.
20. Juno — The Girl in the T-Shirt
I walked over to her.

It was not far. Thirty steps, maybe. Across the edge of the camp, past the wagon with its ribs showing, past the boy drawing in the dirt with his stick, who did not look up. It took me a very long time. The minute opened up in front of me the way minutes had been opening for a month, and I walked into it, and every step was a room.
The hum was louder here. The light was flatter. The ground under my boots was not gravel anymore. It was carpet. Thin gray carpet, worn into paths. I could feel it give.
I sat down in front of her. Cross-legged, in the dirt, on the carpet, whatever it was. Close enough to touch. I did not touch her.
She was still looking at her hands.

Up close I could see everything. The sweat on her upper lip. A smear of something red on her chin, a Popsicle maybe, from before. The dead lights in her sneakers. The yellow T-shirt, Kit’s T-shirt, with a cartoon dog on it, faded nearly white, the neck stretched out so it hung off one of her shoulders. I had worn that shirt until it fell apart. I had forgotten it existed. I had forgotten that I had ever been this small.
Her fingers. The nails were broken. Torn down to the pink. There was dried blood at the corners, brown, and a little bit of something under the nails, gray, like rubber, or vinyl.
“Hey,” I said.
She did not answer.
“I know you,” I said.
She turned her hands over. Looked at the palms. Turned them back.
“I’m sorry,” I said. My voice came out wrong. “I’m sorry I didn’t just get out. I could have just gotten out. I should have opened the door. If I had opened the door, none of it—”
She looked up at me.

Her eyes. I do not know how to tell you about her eyes. They were my eyes, but they were nine, and they were very, very tired, the way only a child who has been waiting a long time can be tired. They looked at me like I had said something stupid. Not cruel. Just stupid. The way you look at a grownup who has got everything backwards.
She held up her hands. Close to my face. So I could see.
And I saw.

I saw the inside of the Buick. The tan seats, cracked, hot enough to burn. The windows up. The air like the inside of a mouth. I saw the door handle, the chrome one on the back door, and I saw my own small hand on it, pulling. Pulling. The handle moving and the door not opening. Because the back doors had the child locks on. Because Mom had put them on years before, when I was little, because I used to open the door on the freeway. Because the back doors of that Buick did not open from the inside. They had never opened from the inside.

I saw myself climb over into the front. I saw the front doors. The lock knobs, pushed down, sunk deep in the doors. I saw myself pull and pull at the front handle, and it did not open either, because the lock was down and the knob was too slippery and too small and my hands were wet, and I was nine.

I saw myself at the window. Scratching at the window. Clawing at the rubber seal around the glass, trying to get my fingers into it, trying to pull the glass down with my nails, the way you try anything when there is nothing to try. I saw the nails bend back and break. I saw the blood on the rubber.

I heard myself screaming. I had never remembered screaming. I screamed until there was nothing left to scream with. And people walked by. In the parking lot of the Rite Aid. People walked by, in the heat, looking at their phones, carrying bags, and nobody heard. Or nobody looked.
And then I saw myself stop. Lie down on the seat. Very tired. The seat burning my cheek. And the light in the car going flat and gray-white, and a hum starting, and the smell of carpet.
The girl put her hands down.
I could not open the door.
I could never open the door.

I had not sat there because I wanted to be good. I had not stayed because he told me to wait. I had not chosen anything. I had fought that car with everything a nine-year-old has, and the car had won, and nobody came. Nobody came for a long, long time.

And afterwards — after the stranger with the rock, after the ambulance and the hospital and the foster homes and Kit taken away — afterwards, some part of me had taken that afternoon and quietly turned it around. Turned it inside out like a shirt. You could have gotten out. You chose to stay. It was you. You did it. For eighteen years I had believed it. I had built my whole life on it, the way you build a house on a floor. I had believed that I was the one who did something wrong, because the truth was that I was the one nothing could be done for. That I was small, and locked in, and screaming, and nobody came.
I would rather have been guilty.
God, I would rather have been guilty.

I do not know how long I sat there. The minute did not end. The girl sat across from me with her broken hands in her lap, and she was not crying, and neither was I, at first. Then I was. Not the way I cry, quietly, so nobody hears. The other way. The way I had not cried since I was nine. The way that comes from the bottom of something and takes your whole body with it.
The girl watched me. After a while she reached out, very slowly, and put one broken finger on the back of my hand. Just one. Light as a fly.
It was hot. Her finger was hot like the inside of that car.
I turned my hand over and held hers. Her whole hand fit inside my palm. I held it the way you hold something you have been looking for under every piece of furniture in the house for eighteen years.
“Okay,” I said. “Okay. I’m here. I’m here now.”
It was a stupid thing to say. It was the only thing.
She did not answer. But she leaned forward, a little, the way a tired child leans, until her forehead was against my shoulder. And she stayed there. And I stayed.
Somewhere behind me, across the camp, a long way off, I heard Abe say my name.
21. Abe — The Asking
I do not know how long I stood in front of Lyle.

He looked the way he looked the morning I left him. Thirty-two. Sunburned across the nose. That stupid grown-out haircut he was always going to cut and never did. He was standing on the broken ankle like it was nothing. Behind him the families sat in the gray light and waited.
“You came,” he said.
“Nineteen years late.”
“Yeah. That’s a lot of late.” He grinned. “Did you bring the truck?”
“I brought a deer cart.”
“Outstanding,” Lyle said, in my voice, exactly my voice, and I laughed, and the laugh broke in the middle and turned into something else.
“I’m sorry,” I said. “Lyle. I said I’d be back by morning.”

“You’d have been back by morning,” he said. “Your heart had other plans. I know. I was here when you came through. The first time. You walked right past me. Didn’t even say hi.” He tapped his chest. “We all saw you, man. You were here four minutes. You looked like you’d lost your car keys.”
I could not say anything.
“I wrote on the rock,” he said. “You see that?”
“They told me.”

“Abe coming.” He shook his head. “I didn’t write it so they’d blame you. I wrote it so they’d know I wasn’t alone. You get that, right? That’s what it meant. I wasn’t sitting there waiting for you to save me. I was sitting there knowing somebody was trying. That’s different. That’s a lot different, Abe.”
My heart was falling down the stairs. Hard now. The pennies in my mouth. My hands were cold and the cold was coming up my arms.

“You walked out,” Lyle said. “And now you walked back in. That’s the whole story. That’s both halves. Nobody reads the sequel. You did.” He looked over my shoulder. “Now you’ve got to walk somebody out. That’s how it ends. Everybody walks out together.”

Behind him, the families were standing up. All of them. Slowly, stiffly, the way people stand after sitting a long time. The women shaking out their skirts. The men lifting the children. The big ox getting his back legs under him and then his front. They were looking west, at the mountains. Toward the pass.
And then the ground came up.

I did not fall the way you fall in the movies. My knees just stopped. I sat down on the carpet, on the gravel, on whatever it was, and then I was lying on my side, and my cheek was on something hot and gritty. The light went flat. My heart was not falling down the stairs anymore. It was at the bottom of the stairs, lying there, twitching.
Oliver was in my ear. Get up, Coldiron. Get up. Is that it? Is that the show?
And the other voice, under him. The quiet one. The one from the valley with the railroad.
You could ask.

I have been asked for help a thousand times. I have carried men. I have given men water out of my own canteen. I have done CPR on a stranger on the shoulder of the 15, the Vegas freeway. I have never, once, in fifty-one years, asked anybody for anything. Not my father. Not my mother. Not the Marine Corps. Not God. It was the only record I still held.
I could hear Juno coming. Running, over the gravel. I could hear her saying my name, again and again, in a voice I had not heard her use.
Her face came down over mine, upside down, blotting out the gray light.
I opened my mouth. It took everything. Everything I had left.
“Juno,” I said. “Carry me.”
22. Juno — The Mule
The truck was where we had left it, thirty-five days before, at the edge of the camp, white with dust. The note was still on the dash.
GONE WALKING. BACK IN FIVE WEEKS. DON’T TOW.
I ran to it with his keys. I got in and turned the key and the truck said click. Just click. Like a tongue against teeth. Five weeks in the heat. The battery was dead.
I sat in the driver’s seat for one second with my hands on the wheel.
Don’t tow, I thought. Very funny, Abe.

No signal. There is never signal at the spring. The road ran past the camp, a pale strip of gravel, empty in both directions as far as I could see, which was not far, because the sun was gone now and the dark was coming down. Thirteen miles to Badwater, north up the gravel and then east across the salt. Further to anything with people. No headlights. Nothing.
So I did what you do.

I unstrapped the water jugs from the one-eyed mule. I laid the pack frame and the tarp across the cart, the way the hunters do it, a bed on two wheels. I got Abe onto it. I do not know how. He is two hundred pounds and I am a hundred and thirty-five. I got my arms under his arms from behind and I dragged him and lifted him and swore at him and he helped a little, with his legs, and then he did not help at all. I strapped him on with the deer straps. His face was gray. His lips were blue in the headlamp. He was breathing. Little shallow breaths, like a dog asleep.
I picked up the handles. I leaned forward into them.
And I walked north, and then east across the salt. Toward Badwater. Toward the lowest place in America. Down.

I walked out onto the road, because the cart could roll on the road. The wheels made a sound on the gravel like rain. Behind me, at the camp, I did not look. I did not need to. I knew they were standing up. All of them. I knew the girl in the yellow shirt was standing at the edge of the shade, watching me go. I knew Lyle was there with his hands in his pockets.
The Shade Seller came at mile two.
He did not walk beside me this time. He was everywhere. He was the whole night.

Put him down, he said. Very gently. Juno. Put him down. He’s dying. He’s going to die whether you drag him or not. You’re going to drag a dead man thirteen miles. Leave him by the road. Somebody will find him in the morning. Walk. You can walk to Badwater by midnight without him. You’ll live. Somebody has to live.
All true.
He’s not your father, the Shade Seller said. He’s not your brother. You knew him for five weeks. He paid you. You don’t owe him anything. You owe yourself. You’ve owed yourself for eighteen years.
True.

The girl, he said. Leave the girl too. You saw her. You’ve seen enough. You don’t have to carry that. Put her down. Put it all down. Put it all down on the side of the road and walk away and nobody will ever, ever know. There’s shade. There’s so much shade. Look.

And he showed me. Pictures of water. One after another, all along the road. A motel pool, blue and glowing. The swimming pool in Delano, when I was ten. A bed. A bus to Vegas with its lights on. The tan Buick at the edge of a lake. A door, open, with a cool dark room behind it, and nobody in it, and nothing to carry.
I did not argue with him.

That was the thing I learned that night, out there on the gravel road below sea level. You cannot win an argument with him. He is better at arguing than you. He has had your whole life to practice. Every reason he gives you is true.
Somewhere around mile four I remembered Abe’s jar.
He had told me about it on the walk back in, one night in the wash, embarrassed, as if he were confessing he still slept with a stuffed animal. I had laughed at him. Now I took the lid off mine.

I did not have much in it. I had never kept anything. But it turned out things had been going in there anyway, without my knowing, for years. Three in the morning on Union Avenue with a pit bull on a chain and a Silverado I hooked up anyway. The fight in Fresno, the one I won, the one where my eye closed in the second round and I fought the third by sound. The pool in Delano. Two hundred and fifty miles to a theme park. The drum solo under my fingers, that night in the mountains. The girl in the yellow shirt, holding my hand.
You did that, I told myself. That was you. This is smaller than that.
It was not smaller. It was much bigger. It did not matter. It worked anyway.

Then I did the other thing he told me. I looked ahead. Not at the road. All the way. I made myself see it: the sign on the cliff at Badwater, white in the first light, and headlights coming down the road, and Abe’s face with color in it. I could see it so clearly I could have walked into it. I kept it there, in front of me, a picture of water I had painted myself, and I walked toward it.

So I let him talk. I let him say all of it, every single word, and I did not answer, and I did not stop walking. Step. Step. The wheels like rain. The handles cutting into my palms until my palms bled and the blood made the handles slippery, and I wrapped my shirt around them and went on in my bra in the dark like a crazy woman, and I did not stop.
He talked for hours.
And then, somewhere around midnight, somewhere around mile ten, he started to repeat himself.

I noticed it the way you notice a song on the radio has come around again. Put him down. You don’t owe him. There’s shade. He had said that. He had said all of that. Nothing new was coming. It was the same mail, over and over, and I had already read it all.
I stopped opening it.

And then, about an hour later, he stopped. Not because I beat him. Because he had nothing left to sell. He had shown me every picture he had. He had given me every reason. He had emptied his whole cart out on the road in front of me, and I had walked past every single thing in it.
He did not leave. I do not think he ever leaves. But he went quiet. And in the quiet, for the first time in my life, I heard something else.
It was not a voice. It was just my own breathing. My feet. The wheels. The man on the cart behind me, breathing too, still breathing. The stars. The salt hissing as it cooled.
It was very loud, and it was very calm. And I was in it. All the way in. Not visiting. Not waiting to leave.
I was living there.
I laughed out loud, alone, on the gravel road, at nothing. I could not have told you what was funny. Something was.
Interlude Ix — The Salt That Stays

When a person first walks into great heat, the body panics a little. The heart races. The sweat pours. And the sweat is salty — so salty you can see it dry white on your skin, on your shirt, on the brim of your hat. The body is throwing away its salt in a hurry, the way a frightened person throws everything out of a boat.
But if the person stays — if they keep walking in the heat, day after day — the body begins to learn.
Within a week or two, the heart beats slower in the same heat. The body starts sweating sooner, and sweats more. And the sweat itself changes.

It carries less salt. The body has learned to hold on to what it needs. Scientists who study soldiers and athletes have measured it, again and again. It is one of the most reliable things the body knows how to do.
It cannot learn this anywhere else. Not in the shade. Not in a cool room reading about heat. Only in the heat, by staying.

People who stay in hard places change in a similar way. Not all at once. The fear does not leave. The pain does not stop hurting. But slowly the body stops panicking. It stops throwing everything overboard. It learns what to keep.
The salt on your skin is the bill for staying.
It is also the receipt.
23. Abe — Somebody Called My Name
I was in the waiting room again.

Same light. Flat and gray-white, from nowhere. Same hum, in the ceiling, in the walls, in my teeth. Same carpet, thin and gray, worn into paths by ten thousand people in bad shoes. Same smell of burnt coffee and breathed air. Same chairs, the plastic ones joined together in rows, orange, with a little shelf at the end with magazines on it. I looked at the magazines. They were the same magazines. Nineteen years, and nobody had changed the magazines.
I sat down. Where else would you sit.

There were other people. There are always other people. Not many. A woman in a bonnet with her hands in her lap. A man in a long coat looking at the floor. A little boy, swinging his legs, drawing on the carpet with his finger.
And Lyle. In the chair next to mine. Like we had come in together.
“Hey,” he said.
“Hey.”
“Told you the magazines were bad.”
“You never told me that.”
“I’m telling you now.” He picked one up and showed me. A Field and Stream from 1987. “I’ve read this four hundred times. There’s an article about bass. I know more about bass than any man alive.”

I laughed. It did not hurt here. Nothing hurt here. That was the thing about the waiting room. My heart was not falling down the stairs. My heart was not doing anything. It was very quiet in my chest, and the quiet was nice, and I understood how a man could sit in that chair for a long time and not mind.
“This is the shade,” I said.
“Yeah,” Lyle said. “This is the best shade there is.”
We sat. The light hummed. The little boy drew on the carpet.
“I like it here,” I said.
“I know you do,” Lyle said. “That’s why you’ve got to go.”
He stood up. He had his old Marine field jacket on, the one with the name tape torn off, the one he had worn on the walk, the one they had found him in. He took it off. He held it out to me.
“It’s cold out there,” he said. “Where you’re going. Nights get cold in November.”
“Lyle.”
“Take the coat, Abe.”
I took the coat. It was warm from him.
“Somebody’s going to call your name,” he said. “Pretty soon. Pretty loud. I’d answer, if I were you.”
“How do you know?”

“Because I can hear her,” Lyle said, and grinned. “Everybody here can hear her. She’s been yelling for twenty minutes. She’s got a mouth on her, Coldiron. She’s using words I didn’t learn in the Corps.”
And then I heard it too.
From very far away. From above. Through the ceiling, through the hum, through nineteen years.
ABE.
Not a nice voice. Not a waiting-room voice. Furious. Hoarse. Ragged. A voice that had been screaming for a long time and had a lot more screaming in it.
ABE. ABE COLDIRON. DON’T YOU DARE. DON’T YOU DARE, YOU GRAY IDIOT. ABE.

And with it, a thump. A thump in my chest, from outside. Hard. And another. And another. Somebody pushing on me, hard and fast, again and again, a hundred times a minute, the way they teach you, the way I had done it on the shoulder of the 15. Every thump, the waiting room shook a little. The magazines slid on the shelf. The light flickered.
ABE. YOU ASKED. YOU ASKED ME, YOU DON’T GET TO ASK AND THEN LEAVE. ABE.
Lyle sat back down. He picked up his Field and Stream. He opened it to the article about bass.
“Somebody called your name,” he said, without looking up. “Go on.”
I stood up. I had the coat in my hands.
“Lyle—”
“Go on, Abe. I’m fine. I’ve got bass.”
I looked at him one more time. At the stupid haircut, and the sunburned nose, and the ankle in its brown bandage, propped up on the chair across from him like a man at home.
Then I turned around and walked toward the voice.

The light got brighter. Real light. Hard, and orange, and coming from one side. The hum turned into something else, a roaring, a wind. The carpet turned to salt, rough and cold under my cheek. And the thumps in my chest stopped being something outside me and became my own heart, kicking, once, twice, and catching, the way an old truck catches, and then going. Going.
I opened my eyes.

Juno was kneeling over me in the dawn, on the salt, with no shirt on and her hands bloody and her hair stuck to her face. Behind her, high on the brown cliff, small as a postage stamp, there was a white sign.
She was crying and swearing at the same time. I did not know a person could do both at once.
I tried to say outstanding. It came out as a sort of croak.
“Don’t,” she said. “Don’t you dare.”
24. Juno — Goodbye

The ranger came at six-forty. A Park Service truck, white with a green stripe, coming down the road from Furnace Creek, the park’s little headquarters town up the valley, on his morning drive to check the bathrooms at Badwater. A young guy with a mustache he had not earned yet. He saw us from a quarter mile off — a woman in a bra kneeling on the salt flats beside a man laid out on the salt next to a deer cart — and he hit the lights.

He had a radio. He had oxygen. He had one of those machines that talk to you and tell you when to shock. Abe did not need the shock. Abe’s heart was going on its own by then, going badly, falling down stairs, but going. The ranger put the mask on him. He called it in. He kept looking at me.
“Ma’am,” he said. “Where did you come from?”
“The spring,” I said. “Bennett’s Well.”
“That’s thirteen miles.”
“Yes.”
“You pulled him thirteen miles?”
“He asked,” I said.

The helicopter came at seven-thirty. It came down out of the sky over the Black Mountains with the sun behind it and landed on the road, and the noise and the wind were enormous, salt blowing everywhere, and two people in flight suits ran out with a stretcher and put Abe on it.

Before they took him, he opened his eyes. He looked at me. His face under the oxygen mask was gray and old and his eyes were very clear. He had something clutched in one hand. A jacket. An old field jacket with the name tape torn off. I had not seen it before. I did not know where it came from. I still do not know.
He could not talk. But he lifted two fingers off the stretcher, a little salute. And I lifted two back.
Then they took him up into the sky.

I stood on the salt and watched the helicopter until it was a dot, and then until it was nothing, going east, toward Las Vegas. The ranger stood beside me. He gave me a bottle of water and a Park Service windbreaker with a patch on the shoulder, and I put it on, and I drank the water. My hands were shaking so hard I could not hold the bottle and he held it for me.
When the noise was gone, it was very quiet.

I turned around and looked at the valley. The whole of it. In the early light, it was gold and white and enormous, the salt going away to the south in great broken plates, the mountains on both sides lit pink at their tops. Somewhere down there, thirteen miles south, was a spring with a little green around it, and some mesquite, and a dead white truck, and a camp.
I could not see them from there. I did not need to.

I knew they had walked out. I knew they had all stood up, and the ox had got its legs under it, and the children had been lifted, and they had walked west, toward the pass. I knew a young man with a broken ankle was walking with them, and that it did not hurt him. I knew a girl in a yellow T-shirt was walking too. I did not know where she was walking to. I hoped it was somewhere with a pool.

There was salt on my arms. White. Crusted. All the way up to the elbows. On my face, I could feel it, on my lips. The salt of thirty-six days, the salt of the road last night, all of it, dried white in the sun.
I said it out loud. I did not mean to. It just came out, the way it must have come out of somebody’s mouth in 1850, standing at the top of the last mountain, looking back.
“Goodbye, Death Valley,” I said.
The ranger looked at me.
“It’s a thing people say,” I told him.
25. Abe — Rent

They kept me in Las Vegas for nine days. Then in Loma Linda [LOH-mah LIN-dah], at the big heart hospital east of Los Angeles, for another eleven. They put a little machine in my chest the size of a matchbox, with a wire into my heart, that will shock it if it ever stops again. They closed the hole I was born with. They used a little umbrella on a wire, through a vein in my leg. The doctor showed me a picture. It looked like something you would put on a Christmas tree.
“You should be dead,” the doctor said. “Twice.”
“Three times,” I said. “You’re not counting the first one.”
She did not laugh. Doctors never do. I have noticed that.
Juno came every day. Every single day. She drove out from wherever she was staying in a car I did not ask about. She sat in the chair by the bed with her feet up on the rail and ate my Jell-O.
“So,” she said, the first day. “What was it like.”
“Waiting room,” I said. “Bad lighting.”
“Did they call your name?”
“Somebody did.”
“Was it a nice voice?”
“No,” I said. “It was the worst voice I ever heard. It swore at me for twenty minutes. It used words they don’t teach in the Corps.”
She looked pleased with herself. “Noted,” she said.

On the fifth day she brought me sunflower seeds. On the seventh she brought me a tiny plastic mule from a gift shop, gray, with a sad face, and drew a single eye on it with a pen and put it on the tray table, where it watched me eat.
On the ninth day I told her about the house.
I did not plan to. It was late. The hospital was quiet in that way hospitals are quiet, which is not quiet at all, just a different kind of noise. Machines. Shoes in the hall. Somebody’s television.
“I built a house down there,” I said. “Nineteen years ago. Below sea level. That’s what I call it, the place I go. When I walked out on
Lyle. I built a house in the worst place I knew and I moved in. I thought that was what you did. You go to the hard place and you stay. You make it your home. I’ve been living there ever since.”
“I know,” Juno said.

“I thought that made me strong. All the races. Badwater. All of it. I thought I was the hardest man alive because I could live down there.” I looked at the ceiling. “I wasn’t living there because I was strong. I was living there because I owed rent. Every mile was a payment. Nineteen years of payments. Never once did I think I’d paid enough.”
She was quiet for a while.
“You asked me,” she said. “On the salt. You asked me to carry you.”
“Yeah.”
“First time?”
“First time in my life.”
“How did it feel?”
I thought about it. I thought about it for a long time. “Like the worst thing that ever happened to me,” I said. “And like setting something down.”
She nodded. She put her hand on the rail of the bed, near mine, not touching.
“The rent’s paid, Abe,” she said.

I looked at her. She meant it. She meant it with her whole face. I loved her for it. I loved her the way you love a person who has dragged you thirteen miles through the dark and then come back every day to eat your Jell-O.

“No, it isn’t,” I said. “That’s the thing nobody tells you. It’s never paid. You don’t get to own a house down there. You only rent. You pay every day you live in it.” I turned my hand over on the blanket. “But you can pay it with somebody else. It turns out that’s allowed. I didn’t know that. Nobody told me that was allowed.”
Juno looked at my hand, palm up on the blanket. Then she put hers in it.

We sat like that until the nurse came in to do my numbers. Then we let go, and Juno ate the last of the Jell-O, and the little one-eyed mule watched us from the tray table with its one drawn eye, surprised, as always, at everything.
26. Juno — Below Sea Level
I played it in a motel room outside Barstow.

The Desert Sands Motor Lodge, room nine. Abe had gone home that afternoon to his house in Barstow with his new heart and his little machine and his field jacket, which he would not take off and would not explain. I had driven him there and carried his bag in and refused to stay for dinner, and he had not asked me to, because he is still Abe, and then at the door he had asked me to anyway, because he is not exactly Abe anymore. I said not tonight. I said I had a thing.
I had a thing.

The room had a bed with a brown cover and a painting of a sailboat over it, and a window unit that rattled, and a carpet that was thin and gray and worn into paths. I noticed the carpet. I made myself notice it, and I made myself stay, and I sat down on the end of the bed in my boots.

There was still salt in the creases of my hands. I could not get it all out. I had washed and washed and it was still there, white in the lines of my palms, in the skin around my nails. I looked at it for a while.
Then I took out the phone.
The little red number. One. Two years and fifty-one days.
I pressed it. I held the phone to my ear. I heard the click. I heard him breathe in.
And this time I did not press stop.
Hey. Juno. It’s — it’s Kit. I don’t know if this is still your number. A lady at the county gave it to me. She wasn’t supposed to.
His voice was older. Deeper. Rough at the edges like something that had been sanded by hand. But it was his. Under all of it, it was his. I would have known it at the bottom of the ocean.
I’m — okay. I’m going to just say it. I’m in a program. I’ve been sober eleven months. Part of it is, you’re supposed to — you’re supposed to go to the people. And say it. So I’m saying it.
A breath. A long one. I could hear a car go by wherever he was. I could hear a dog.

That day. At the Rite Aid. I wasn’t stealing. I mean I was. I was stealing. But I got caught right away. Like ten minutes in. And the guy took me in the back and he was going to call the cops and I was so scared, Juno. I was fourteen. And I didn’t tell him. I didn’t tell him you were in the car. I kept thinking I’d get out, I’d talk my way out, I’d get back before — and I didn’t tell him. For three hours I didn’t tell him.
The window unit rattled. I did not move.
And then I heard the sirens. From the back room. And I knew. I knew it was for you. And I still — I sat there. I just sat there. And I let them come.
He stopped. For a long time there was only breathing. His and mine. I realized I was breathing with him. In and out. Two years apart.
I’m sorry I left you in the car.
He said it very simply. Like a man setting something heavy on a floor.

I’m sorry I left you in the car. It was me. It was never you. I need you to know that, even if you never — even if you don’t call. It was me. You were nine. You couldn’t — those doors didn’t even open. Mom put the locks on. You couldn’t have gotten out. You know that, right? I don’t know what they told you. I don’t know what you told yourself. It wasn’t you, Juno.
I’m in Bakersfield. On Ming. The blue house by the 99. If you ever — I’m here. I’m just here. Okay.
Okay. Bye.
The click.
I sat there.
I played it again.

I played it eleven times. I know because I counted. I sat on the end of the bed in room nine of the Desert Sands Motor Lodge with the sailboat over my head and the carpet under my boots and I played it again and again, until I knew every breath in it, every car going by, the dog, the place where his voice went up like a boy’s on the word nine.
Then I got up and got in the car.

It is a hundred and thirty miles from Barstow to Bakersfield. West on the 58, over the Tehachapis [tuh-HATCH-uh-peez], the mountains that wall off the valley, down into the valley. I have driven it a hundred times. I drove it that night like I had never seen it.
The Shade Seller got in at Boron, the borax-mine town an hour out.

I had not heard him since the road. Since mile ten, since midnight, since the cart. I had thought maybe he was gone. He was not gone. He is never gone. He got in on the passenger side like an old friend I had given a ride to before, and he settled in, and he was gentle, gentler than he had ever been, because he knew this was the last chance he was going to get.
You don’t have to go tonight, he said. It’s late. He’s probably asleep. Go in the morning.
True.
You could text him. That’s what people do now. Send a text. Let him come to you. You’ve done enough coming.
True.

He left you in that car for three hours, Juno. He heard the sirens and he sat there. You don’t owe him a knock on his door. You don’t owe him anything. You never did. You found that out. That’s what you found out. So why are you driving toward him?
True. Every word.

You’ve been through enough. You’ve walked five hundred miles. You died on a car seat and you came back and you dragged a dying man thirteen miles across the bottom of the world. Isn’t that enough? When is it enough? Turn around. Go back to Barstow. Abe asked you to dinner. Go have dinner. Be happy for once. There’s shade. There’s so much shade, Juno. Look. Look how much shade.
And it was all true. All of it. He had never lied to me. Not once. Not in the desert, not on the road, not now.
I pulled over at Tehachapi. On the shoulder, with the trucks going by and shaking the car, and the wind up there coming over the pass hard and cold. I sat with my hands on the wheel.
I let him talk.
I did not argue. I had learned that on the road. You do not argue with him. You cannot. I just let him say all of it, every true thing, and I sat there and let each one land, and I did not answer.

Then I laughed. I do not know what at. At him, maybe. At me. At a woman sitting on the shoulder of the 58 at eleven at night, with salt in her hands, listening to nobody, and losing, and going anyway.
“Noted,” I said out loud, to the empty passenger seat.
And I pulled back out onto the road.

I am going to tell you what I knew, on that drive down out of the mountains, with the lights of Bakersfield coming up out of the dark ahead of me like something spilled. Because it is the only thing I know for sure, and it took me thirty-six days and five hundred miles and one brother on a voicemail and one little girl in a yellow T-shirt to find it out.

I was not going there to be forgiven. There was nothing to forgive me for. That was the whole thing. That was what the girl had shown me with her broken nails. I had spent eighteen years apologizing for something I never did, because it was easier than the truth.
And I was not going there to forgive him. I did not know if I could. Maybe someday. Maybe not. I could not tell you. I still cannot.
I was going because the truth was worse than the lie, and I had to stand in it.

That is all. That was the whole reason. For eighteen years I had kept myself out of that car by telling myself I chose to be in it. I had built a house on that. A whole life. Sleeping in other people’s cars. Taking things off people’s driveways in the dark and driving away. Never staying anywhere long enough for anybody to knock on the door. And all that time, the truth was sitting there, at the edge of the camp, in the heat, with broken nails, waiting for somebody to come and sit down with her.
The truth was that I was small, and locked in, and I screamed, and nobody came.
That is the worst place I know. That is the bottom. Lower than Badwater. Lower than anything with a sign.
And I was driving into it on purpose.

Not to fix it. You cannot fix it. Not to get out the other side. There is no other side. Just to go there. Just to stand in it with my eyes open, and not leave. To live there for a while, in the worst place I know, and find out what kind of house a person can build at the bottom of everything.

Ming Avenue at one in the morning. The 99, the big valley freeway, roaring behind the houses like the sea. A blue house with a chain-link fence and a light on over the porch, a yellow bug light, with moths going around it.
I parked. I got out. I walked up the path.

The porch had three steps. They were concrete, and one of them was cracked, and there was a pot of something dead at the top of them. There was a doormat that said nothing. There was a screen door with a hole in it near the bottom, where a dog had pushed through.
I stood on the doormat.

My heart was going so hard I could feel it in my teeth. In my fingertips. The way Abe’s went, that night in the mountains, falling down the stairs. I stood there and let it go. I did not try to stop it.
I thought about the sign at Badwater. That little white sign, way up on the cliff. SEA LEVEL. And all of us down underneath it, looking up.
Bakersfield is four hundred feet above the sea. I know that. I looked it up once, at the tow yard, on a slow night. Four hundred feet up.
I have never been lower in my life.

The Shade Seller did not say anything. He was standing on the step behind me. I could feel him there. But he had nothing left to sell. He had shown me every picture of water he owned. He had given me every true reason in the world. And I was still here, on the mat, with the moths going around the light.
I looked at my hand.
There was still salt in it. White, in the lines of the palm. I could not get it out. I do not think I ever will.
I raised it, and I knocked.
I’m below sea level.
I think I’ll stay a while.

GLOSSARY
Amargosa [aa-mar-GO-sah] — Spanish, bitter. The river that runs south out of Nevada and turns into Death Valley, where it sinks into the ground and does not come out.
Arcan, Jean-Baptiste [zhahn bah-TEEST ar-KAHN] — A
Frenchman who waited at the 1849 camp with his wife Abigail and their small son Charles until Manly and Rogers came back for them.
Badwater — The lowest point in North America, a salt flat on the floor of Death Valley, 282 feet below sea level. A sign high on the cliff above it marks where the sea would be.

Below Sea Level — Abe’s name for the hard place, which Juno takes up: the state the mind and body enter under great discomfort, of either kind, where everything sits lower than where you started and nothing drains away.
Bennett’s Well — A spring on the floor of Death Valley, near the camp where the Bennett and Arcan families waited in the winter of 1849 for Manly and Rogers to return.
Black Mountains — The range on the east side of Death Valley, behind Badwater; the sun comes up over it.
Building a house down there — Staying in the hard place long enough to stop waiting to leave it; getting used to living in discomfort rather than visiting it.
Deer cart — A two-wheeled frame with handles, sold to hunters for dragging game out of rough country. Abe draws one eye on his and calls it the mule.
Furnace Creek — The park’s small headquarters town, up the valley from Badwater.
Goodbye, Death Valley — The words said to have been spoken by a member of the 1849 party as they climbed out of the valley for the last time, and the origin of its name.
The jar — Abe’s name for the place in his head where he keeps every hard thing he has come through, to take one out and look at it when he needs it.
Kosovo [KOH-soh-voh] — A small country in the Balkans, in south-eastern Europe, where American Marines were sent as peacekeepers in 1999.
Loma Linda [LOH-mah LIN-dah] — Spanish, pretty hill. A town east of Los Angeles with a large heart hospital.

Manly and Rogers — William Lewis Manly and John Rogers, the two young men who walked roughly two hundred and fifty miles out of Death Valley for help in the winter of 1849, and then walked back in to bring the families out.
Old Crump — The ox who carried the Bennett children out of
Death Valley, and whom Asabel Bennett swore he would never eat.
Panamint — The mountain range on the west side of Death Valley, and the valley beyond it.

Pictures of Water — The mind’s way of showing a way out: a pain that is not damage yet, a buried memory, a very good reason to stop. Named after the desert mirage, which is a piece of sky bent by heat until it lies on the ground.
Pristina [PRISH-tee-nah] — The capital of Kosovo.
Rancho San Francisco [RAHN-cho san fran-SIS-ko] — Spanish,
Saint Francis ranch. The cattle ranch north of Los Angeles where Manly and Rogers found food in 1850. The ground near it now holds a theme park.
Salt — What is left on the skin when sweat burns off in great heat; in this book, what stays in a person who has stayed in the hard place.
The Shade Seller — Juno’s name for the voice that wants you out of the hard place. He is friendly, patient and never lies. The shade he sells is real, and the price is that you stop walking.
Tehachapi [tuh-HATCH-uh-pee] — The mountains between the
Mojave Desert and the Central Valley, crossed by the 58 on the way to Bakersfield.
Trona — A company town on the edge of a dry lake west of Death
Valley, where salt, soda and borax are taken out of the old lakebed.
